arXiv:2502.05993v2 [math.NT] 17 Jan 2026

Hankel continued fractions
and Hankel determinants
for qq-deformed metallic numbers

Guo-Niu Han Address: Guo-Niu Han, Université de Strasbourg, CNRS, IRMA, UMR 7501, Strasbourg, France Email address: guoniu.han@unistra.fr and Emmanuel Pedon Address: Emmanuel Pedon, Université de Reims Champagne-Ardenne, CNRS, LMR, UMR 9008, Reims, France Email address: emmanuel.pedon@univ-reims.fr
Date: 07/02/2025
Abstract.

Fix nn a positive integer. Take the nn-th metallic number

ϕn=n+n2+42\phi_{n}=\frac{n+\sqrt{n^{2}+4}}{2}

(e.g. ϕ1\phi_{1} is the golden number) and let Φn​(q)\Phi_{n}(q) be its qq-deformation in the sense of S. Morier-Genoud & V. Ovsienko. This is an algebraic continued fraction which admits an expansion into a Taylor series Φn​(q)=∑i=0+∞fi​qi\Phi_{n}(q)=\sum_{i=0}^{+\infty}f_{i}q^{i} around q=0q=0, with integral coefficients. Consider the sequences of shifted Hankel determinants of Φn\Phi_{n}:

Δj(ℓ):=det(fa+b+ℓ)a,b=0j−1,ℓ,j⩾0.\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)}:=\det(f_{a+b+\ell})_{a,b=0}^{j-1},\quad\ell,j\geqslant 0.

By using the notion of Hankel continued fraction introduced by the first author in [Han16] we determine explicitly the first n+2n+2 sequences Δj(0),Δj(1),…,Δj(n+1)\Delta_{j}^{(0)},\Delta_{j}^{(1)},\dots,\Delta_{j}^{(n+1)} and show that they satisfy the following properties:

  1. 1)

    They are periodic and consist of −1,0,1-1,0,1 only.

  2. 2)

    They satisfy a three-term Gale-Robinson recurrence, i.e. they form discrete integrable dynamical systems.

  3. 3)

    They are all completely determined by the first sequence Δj(0)\Delta_{j}^{(0)}.

This article thus validates a conjecture formulated by V. Ovsienko and the second author in [OP25] and establishes new connections between qq-deformations of real numbers and sequences of Catalan or Motzkin numbers.

Key words and phrases:
Hankel determinants, Hankel continued fractions, metallic numbers, golden ratio, qq-analogues, quadratic irrationals, Gale-Robinson sequences.

1. Introduction

Given a power series F⁡(q)=∑i=0+∞fi​qiF(q)=\sum_{i=0}^{+\infty}f_{i}q^{i} or simply a sequence of numbers F=(fi)i∈ℤ⩾0F=(f_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}}, by the Hankel determinants of FF we mean the doubly indexed family

(1.1) Δj(ℓ)​(F):=|fℓfℓ+1⋯fℓ+j−1fℓ+1fℓ+2⋯fℓ+jfℓ+j−1fℓ+j⋯fℓ+2​j−2|\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j}(F):=\left|\begin{matrix}{f}_{\ell}&{f}_{\ell+1}&\cdots&{f}_{\ell+j-1}\\[4.0pt] {f}_{\ell+1}&{f}_{\ell+2}&\cdots&{f}_{\ell+j}\\[4.0pt] \vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\ {f}_{\ell+j-1}&{f}_{\ell+j}&\cdots&{f}_{\ell+2j-2}\end{matrix}\right|

where ℓ,j∈ℤ⩾0\ell,j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}, with the convention Δ0(ℓ)​(F):=1\Delta^{(\ell)}_{0}(F):=1. The determinant Δj(ℓ)​(F)\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j}(F) is thus of size j×jj\times j, and we call the number ℓ\ell the shift of the determinant, since it is clear that

OPENOPENΔj(ℓ)​((fi)i⩾0))=Δj(0)​((fi+ℓ)i⩾0)).\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j}\bigl((f_{i})_{i\geqslant 0})\bigr)=\Delta_{j}^{(0)}\bigl((f_{i+\ell})_{i\geqslant 0})\bigr).

Similarly, if F⁡(q)=∑i=0∞fi​qiF(q)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}f_{i}q^{i} is a power series, we have

(1.2) Δj(ℓ)​(F)=Δj(0)​(F(ℓ))\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j}(F)=\Delta_{j}^{(0)}(F^{(\ell)})

where

F(ℓ)​(q):=1qℓ​(F⁡(q)−∑i=0ℓ−1fi​qi)=1qℓ​(∑i=ℓ+∞fi​qi).F^{(\ell)}(q):=\frac{1}{q^{\ell}}\left(F(q)-\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}f_{i}q^{i}\right)=\frac{1}{q^{\ell}}\left(\sum_{i=\ell}^{+\infty}f_{i}q^{i}\right).

When ℓ=0\ell=0, we will often use the shorter notation Δj​(F)\Delta_{j}(F) instead of Δj(0)​(F)\Delta^{(0)}_{j}(F) and we speak of ordinary Hankel determinants of FF. On the other hand we will write simply Δ(ℓ)​(F)\Delta^{(\ell)}(F) to denote the entire sequence (Δj(ℓ)​(F))j⩾0(\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j}(F))_{j\geqslant 0}.

First appeared in 1861 [H61], Hankel matrices and determinants (and later on, Hankel and Toeplitz operators) are this kind of objects that arise naturally in various fields of mathematics and often interconnect them: combinatorics [Rad79, Aig99, Tam01, CK11], orthogonal polynomials [Vie83, Jun03, DIK11, BP17], number theory [Wal48, APWW98, Bug11], probability theory [Sch17, BDJ06], complex analysis [Hen74, Pom66, KLS18], functional and applied analysis [Pel03, Sau21]… (among many other valuable references).

In this article we would like to present the remarkable properties of Hankel determinants of a family of power series Φn\Phi_{n} (n∈ℤ⩾1n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 1}) that are defined as “qq-deformations”, in the sense of S. Morier-Genoud and V. Ovsienko (to be specified a bit later), of the so-called metallic numbers, or metallic ratios, or metallic means. Recall that these numbers are the quadratic irrationals

ϕn:=n+n2+42=n+1n+1n+1⋱,n⩾1,\phi_{n}:=\frac{n+\sqrt{n^{2}+4}}{2}=n+\cfrac{1}{n+\cfrac{1}{n+\cfrac{1}{\ddots}}},\quad n\geqslant 1,

with most famous representatives:

ϕ1\displaystyle\phi_{1} =1+52(golden ratio),\displaystyle=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\qquad\text{(golden ratio)},
ϕ2\displaystyle\phi_{2} =1+2(silver ratio),\displaystyle=1+\sqrt{2}\qquad\text{(silver ratio)},
ϕ3\displaystyle\phi_{3} =3+132(bronze ratio).\displaystyle=\frac{3+\sqrt{13}}{2}\qquad\text{(bronze ratio)}.

Surprisingly, the properties of their Hankel determinants, together with some particular continued fraction expansions, will make our functions Φn\Phi_{n} resemble to the generating series of Catalan or Motzkin numbers, which are ubiquitous in mathematics. This connection was first observed in cases n=1n=1 and n=2n=2 by V. Ovsienko and the second author [OP25]. The present work is thus a continuation and generalization of the results therein.

Let us elaborate. First, we recall that the Catalan numbers are defined by the formula11 1 We avoid the traditional notation CnC_{n} because of possible confusion with some other object introduced later.

(1.3) γn:=1n+1​(2​nn)=(2​n)!n!​(n+1)!,n⩾0,\gamma_{n}:=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}=\frac{(2n)!}{n!(n+1)!},\quad n\geqslant 0,

and that first terms are

1,1,2,5,14,42,132,429,1430,4862,16796,58786,208012,742900,2674440,…1,1,2,5,14,42,132,429,1430,4862,16796,58786,208012,742900,2674440,\,\ldots

see sequence A000108 in the On-line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS) [OEI25]. All shifted Hankel determinants of the generating series Γ⁡(q):=∑n=0+∞γn​qn\Gamma(q):=\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty}\gamma_{n}q^{n} are known, and expressed by the following simple formulas (see e.g. [Aig99, DCV86, Kra05]):

(1.4) Δj​(Γ)=1, 1, 1, 1,…,\displaystyle\Delta_{j}(\Gamma)=1,\,1,\,1,\,1,\,\ldots, Δj(1)​(Γ)\displaystyle\Delta^{(1)}_{j}(\Gamma) =1, 1, 1, 1,…,\displaystyle=1,\,1,\,1,\,1,\,\ldots,
(1.5) Δj(2)​(Γ)=1, 2, 3, 4,…,\displaystyle\Delta^{(2)}_{j}(\Gamma)=1,\,2,\,3,\,4,\,\ldots, Δj(ℓ)​(Γ)\displaystyle\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j}(\Gamma) =∏1⩽a⩽b⩽ℓ−12​j+a+ba+b,ℓ⩾2.\displaystyle=\prod_{1\leqslant a\leqslant b\leqslant\ell-1}\frac{2j+a+b}{a+b},\quad\ell\geqslant 2.

Another classical example is that of the Motzkin numbers

Mn:=∑k=0⌊n/2⌋(n2​k)​γk,n⩾0,M_{n}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\binom{n}{2k}\gamma_{k},\quad n\geqslant 0,

that form sequence A001006 in OEIS:

1,1,2,4,9,21,51,127,323,835,2188,5798,15511,41835,113634,…1,1,2,4,9,21,51,127,323,835,2188,5798,15511,41835,113634,\,\ldots

In this case, the first four sequences of Hankel determinants of the generating series M⁡(q):=∑n=0+∞Mn​qnM(q):=\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty}M_{n}q^{n} are given by

(1.6) Δj​(M)\displaystyle\Delta_{j}(M) =1, 1, 1, 1,…,\displaystyle=1,\,1,\,1,\,1,\,\ldots,
(1.7) Δj(1)​(M)\displaystyle\Delta^{(1)}_{j}(M) =1, 1, 0,−1,−1, 0,1, 1, 0,−1,−1, 0,…,\displaystyle=1,\,1,\,0,-1,-1,\,0,1,\,1,\,0,-1,-1,\,0,\,\ldots,
(1.8) Δj(2)​(M)\displaystyle\Delta^{(2)}_{j}(M) =1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8,…,\displaystyle=1,\,2,\,2,\,3,\,4,\,4,\,5,\,6,\,6,\,7,\,8,\,8,\,\ldots,
Δj(3)​(M)\displaystyle\Delta^{(3)}_{j}(M) =1,4,3,−6,−16,−10,15,36,21,−28,−64,−36,45,…,\displaystyle=1,4,3,-6,-16,-10,15,36,21,-28,-64,-36,45,\,\ldots,

see e.g. [Aig98, BP17]. It is particularly interesting to note that the sequence (1.6) of ordinary Hankel determinants is identically 11 as for Catalan numbers, while the first shifted sequence (1.7) is 33-antiperiodic (thus 66-periodic) and consists of −1,0-1,0, and 11 only (see entry A010892 in OEIS). The sequences Δ(ℓ)​(Φn)\Delta^{(\ell)}(\Phi_{n}) we are going to consider in the present article share this special property, as will be explained below. For later comparison, let us mention also that the shifted Hankel sequence Δn(1)​(M)\Delta^{(1)}_{n}(M) satisfies the recurrence relation

(1.9) Δn+2​Δn=Δn+12−1.\Delta_{n+2}\Delta_{n}=\Delta_{n+1}^{2}-1.

Let us come to the presentation of our results. Throughout the paper we will use the following classical notation for continued fractions:

α0β0+α1β1+α2β2+⋯+αp−1βp−1+αpβp:=α0β0+α1β1+α2⋱+αp−1βp−1+αpβp\frac{\alpha_{0}}{\beta_{0}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{\alpha_{p-1}}{\beta_{p-1}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{\alpha_{p}}{\beta_{p}}:=\cfrac{\alpha_{0}}{\beta_{0}+\cfrac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}+\cfrac{\alpha_{2}}{\ddots+\cfrac{\alpha_{p-1}}{\beta_{p-1}+\cfrac{\alpha_{p}}{\beta_{p}}}}}}

and, to shorten, Gauss’ notation

𝒦j=0p⁡αjβj:=α0β0+α1β1+⋯+αpβp.\mathop{\vphantom{\sum}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{367007}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{262148}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}}\displaylimits_{j=0}^{p}\frac{\alpha_{j}}{\beta_{j}}:=\frac{\alpha_{0}}{\beta_{0}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{\alpha_{p}}{\beta_{p}}.

Both notation are extended to infinite continued fractions, and periodic data inside a continued fraction will be indicated between parentheses and with a star superscript ∗*. For instance, we remind the noticeable expression of the metallic number ϕn\phi_{n} as a 11-periodic regular continued fraction:

ϕn=n+(1n+)∗=n+1n+1n+1n+⋯\phi_{n}=n+\left(\frac{1}{n}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*}=n+\frac{1}{n}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{n}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{n}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}

From now on, for any positive integer nn we denote by Φn\Phi_{n} the qq-deformation of ϕn\phi_{n} in the sense of S. Morier-Genoud and V. Ovsienko [MGO22]. By definition, it is the 2-periodic continued fraction

(1.10) Φn​(q)=[n]q+(qn[n]q−1+q−n[n]q+)∗\Phi_{n}(q)=[n]_{q}+\left(\frac{q^{n}}{[n]_{q^{-1}}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{-n}}{[n]_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*}

where [n]q[n]_{q} is the polynomial which stands for the classical Euler-Gauss qq-deformation of the integer nn:

[n]q:=1−qn1−q=1+q+q2+⋯+qn−1.[n]_{q}:=\frac{1-q^{n}}{1-q}=1+q+q^{2}+\cdots+q^{n-1}.

The functions Φn\Phi_{n} (n⩾1n\geqslant 1) will be refered to as the qq-deformed metallic numbers, or simply the qq-metallic numbers. A motivation for definition (1.10), and more generally for the qq-deformation of real numbers that was discovered by S. Morier-Genoud and V. Ovsienko a few years ago, will be given in Section 2.1, together with some of the key results of the theory.

As an example, let us look at the qq-golden number Φ1​(q)\Phi_{1}(q), i.e. the qq-deformation of the golden ratio ϕ1=1+52\phi_{1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}, whose definition (1.10) can easily be rewritten as

Φ1​(q)=1+(q2q+11+)∗.\Phi_{1}(q)=1+\left(\frac{q^{2}}{q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*}.

In the articles [MGO22] and [OP25] were discovered several striking properties of Φ1\Phi_{1} which led to a comparison with the generating series Γ\Gamma and MM of the Catalan and Motzkin numbers. Let us indicate three such connections:

  1. 1)

    Φ1​(q)\Phi_{1}(q) has various nice continued fraction expansions, such as

    (1.11) Φ1​(q)=11+(−q21+q1+)∗=1+q21+(q1+q1+q31+)∗\Phi_{1}(q)=\frac{1}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\left(\frac{-q^{2}}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*}=1+\frac{q^{2}}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\left(\frac{q}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{3}}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*}

    which belong to the particular class of CC-fractions (see [OP25], where more expansions of Φ1​(q)\Phi_{1}(q), e.g. as JJ-fractions, can also be found). Compare with the following well-known Catalan and Motzkin CC-fraction expansions:

    Γ⁡(q)=11+(−q1+)∗,M⁡(q)=11+(−q1+−q1+−q21+)∗.\Gamma(q)=\frac{1}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\left(\frac{-q}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*},\qquad M(q)=\frac{1}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\left(\frac{-q}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-q}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-q^{2}}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*}.
  2. 2)

    The qq-golden number admits the following Taylor series expansion about q=0q=0:

    (1.12) Φ1​(q)=1+q2−q3+2​q4−4​q5+8​q6−17​q7+37​q8−82​q9+ 185​q10−423​q11+978​q12−2283​q13+5373​q14−12735​q15+⋯\begin{split}\Phi_{1}(q)&=1+q^{2}-q^{3}+2q^{4}-4q^{5}+8q^{6}-17q^{7}+37q^{8}-82q^{9}\\ &\quad+\,185q^{10}-423q^{11}+978q^{12}-2283q^{13}+5373q^{14}-12735q^{15}+\cdots\\ \end{split}

    see [MGO22]. The coefficients here are quite close to sequence A004148 of OEIS, whose terms are called ‘‘generalized Catalan numbers’’22 2 Note however that there are many other sequences known under this name.; the differences are the lack of linear term in the above formula and the alternating signs. Sequence A004148 has many interesting combinatorial interpretations, such as enumeration of peakless Motzkin paths, secondary structures of RNA molecules and diagonal sums of the Narayana triangle, see entry A004148 of [OEI25].

  3. 3)

    Hankel determinants of Φ1\Phi_{1} satisfy the following properties (see [OP25]): the first four sequences of Hankel determinants Δn(ℓ)​(Φ1)\Delta^{(\ell)}_{n}(\Phi_{1}), for ℓ=0,1,2,3\ell=0,1,2,3, are 44-antiperiodic (thus 88-periodic):

    (1.13) Δn+4(ℓ)(Φ1)=−Δn(ℓ)(Φ1),ℓ=0,1,2,3,\Delta^{(\ell)}_{n+4}(\Phi_{1})=-\Delta^{(\ell)}_{n}(\Phi_{1}),\quad\ell=0,1,2,3,

    and they consist of 0,10,1, and −1-1 only. First terms are:

    (1.14) Δj​(Φ1)=1, 1, 1,  0,−1,−1,−1, 0,…,Δj(1)​(Φ1)=1, 0,−1, 1,−1, 0, 1,−1,…,Δj(2)​(Φ1)=1, 1, 1, 0,−1,−1,−1, 0,…,Δj(3)​(Φ1)=1,−1, 0, 0,−1, 1, 0, 0,….\begin{array}[]{rclrrrrrrrr}\Delta_{j}(\Phi_{1})&=&1,&\,1,&\,1,&\;\;0,&-1,&-1,&-1,&\,0,&\ldots,\\ \Delta^{(1)}_{j}(\Phi_{1})&=&1,&\,0,&-1,&\;1,&-1,&\,0,&\,1,&-1,&\ldots,\\ \Delta^{(2)}_{j}(\Phi_{1})&=&1,&\,1,&\,1,&\,0,&-1,&-1,&-1,&\,0,&\ldots,\\ \Delta^{(3)}_{j}(\Phi_{1})&=&1,&-1,&\,0,&\,0,&-1,&\,1,&\,0,&\,0,&\ldots.\end{array}

    These sequences compare with the Motzkin first shifted Hankel sequence (1.7). To some extent, a sequence identically equal to 11 such as (1.4) or (1.6) can be thought of as a particular case of a periodic sequence with values in the set {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\}, thus we may interpret (1.14) as another connection between the qq-golden number Φ1\Phi_{1} and the Catalan and Motzkin series Γ\Gamma and MM. Also, one has

    Δn(4)​(Φ1)=1, 2, 0,−2,−3,−4, 0, 4, 5, 6, 0,−6,−7,−8, 0, 8,…,\Delta^{(4)}_{n}(\Phi_{1})=1,\,2,\,0,-2,-3,-4,\,0,\,4,\,5,\,6,\,0,-6,-7,-8,\,0,\,8,\ldots,

    which reminds (1.5) and (1.8). Lastly, the first three Hankel determinants sequences Δn​(Φ1)\Delta_{n}(\Phi_{1}), Δn(1)​(Φ1)\Delta_{n}^{(1)}(\Phi_{1}) and Δn(2)​(Φ1)\Delta_{n}^{(2)}(\Phi_{1}) all satisfy the Somos-4 relation

    (1.15) Δn+4​Δn=Δn+3​Δn+1−Δn+22,\Delta_{n+4}\Delta_{n}=\Delta_{n+3}\Delta_{n+1}-\Delta_{n+2}^{2},

    which is close to (1.9). Recall that, for k⩾4k\geqslant 4, a Somos-kk sequence is a solution (Sj)(S_{j}) of a quadratic recurrence of the form

    (1.16) Sj​Sj+k=∑i=1⌊k/2⌋αi​Sj+i​Sj+k−iS_{j}S_{j+k}=\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor{k/2}\rfloor}\alpha_{i}S_{j+i}S_{j+k-i}

    for arbitrary integers αi\alpha_{i} and initial data S0,…,Sk−1S_{0},\ldots,S_{k-1}; see more on that subject after the statement of Theorem C below.

Let us say a word about the proofs of (1.13), (1.14) and (1.15). Usual techniques to compute Hankel determinants of classical sequences (such as Catalan or Motzkin) rely mostly on continued fraction expansions, orthogonal polynomials theory and/or combinatorial models; see e.g. [Hei46, Kra99, Kra05, Aig01, Bar10, Elo15, BP17]… In particular, one may think that continued fraction expansions like (1.11) can help to compute the Hankel sequences, since there exists a well-known Hankel determinant formula for regular CC-fractions (also known as Stieltjes continued fractions) and for regular JJ-fractions (also known as Jacobi continued fractions); see [Kra05] §5.4. Unfortunately, it is not possible to expand Φ1\Phi_{1} (nor any Φn\Phi_{n}, actually) as such special continued fractions. But, in [OP25] as well as in the present work, Hankel determinant formulas are obtained by using the notion of Hankel continued fractions introduced by the first author in [Han16]. These form a family of continued fractions which includes both classical regular JJ-fractions and regular CC-fractions as subcases, and still conveniently comes with an explicit Hankel determinant formula; see Section 2.2 for details.

For instance, it was proved in [OP25] (Lemmas 3.6 and 3.9) that the HH-fraction of the qq-golden number Φ1\Phi_{1} is the 33-periodic continued fraction

(1.17) Φ1​(q)=11+(−q21+q+q31+q−q2+q31+q+)∗\Phi_{1}(q)=\frac{1}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\left(\frac{-q^{2}}{1+q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{3}}{1+q-q^{2}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{3}}{1+q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*}

while the HH-fraction expansion of the qq-silver number Φ2\Phi_{2} is 88-periodic and reads:

(1.18) Φ2​(q)=11−q+(q21+q+q21+q21+−q31+2​q2+CLOSEOPENq51+2​q2−q3+q51+2​q2+−q31+q21+)∗.\begin{split}\Phi_{2}(q)=\frac{1}{1-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,&\left(\frac{q^{2}}{1+q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{2}}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{2}}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-q^{3}}{1+2q^{2}}\right.\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\\ &\qquad\left.\frac{q^{5}}{1+2q^{2}-q^{3}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{5}}{1+2q^{2}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-q^{3}}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{2}}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*}.\end{split}

It turns out that these two formulas (and their analogues for the shifts Φ1(ℓ)\Phi_{1}^{(\ell)} and Φ2(ℓ)\Phi_{2}^{(\ell)}), together with the Hankel determinant formula for HH-fractions, yielded all the nice properties of the determinants Δj(ℓ)​(Φ1)\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)}(\Phi_{1}) and Δj(ℓ)​(Φ2)\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)}(\Phi_{2}) that were highlighted in [OP25].

In the present paper we will follow the same path and begin our work by proving the generalization of (1.18) to any integer n⩾2n\geqslant 2, namely:

Theorem A (HH-fraction expansion for Φn\Phi_{n}).

Suppose n⩾2n\geqslant 2 and define the polynomial

(1.19) ⟨n⟩q\displaystyle\langle n\rangle_{q} :=q​[n]q+(1+qn)​(1−q)\displaystyle:=q[n]_{q}+(1+q^{n})(1-q)
={1+q2+q3+⋯+qn−1+2​qn−qn+1, if ​n⩾3,1+2​q2−q3, if ​n=2.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1+q^{2}+q^{3}+\cdots+q^{n-1}+2q^{n}-q^{n+1},&\text{ if }n\geqslant 3,\\ 1+2q^{2}-q^{3},&\text{ if }n=2.\end{cases}

The HH-fraction expansion of the qq-deformed metallic number Φn​(q)\Phi_{n}(q) defined in eq. 1.10 is (6​n−4)(6n-4)-periodic with offset 11 and has the following form:

(1.20) Φn​(q)=11−q+(Un​(q)+Vn​(q)+Wn​(q)+)∗,\Phi_{n}(q)=\frac{1}{1-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\left(U_{n}(q)\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,V_{n}(q)\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,W_{n}(q)\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*},

where

Un​(q)\displaystyle U_{n}(q) =𝒦i=0n−3⁡(qn−i[n−i]q+qn[i+2]q−q+qi+21−q)+q2[2]q+qn[n]q−q+qn1,\displaystyle=\mathop{\vphantom{\sum}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{367007}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{262148}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}}\displaylimits_{i=0}^{n-3}\left(\frac{q^{n-i}}{[n-i]_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{n}}{[i+2]_{q}-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{i+2}}{1-q}\right)\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{2}}{[2]_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{n}}{[n]_{q}-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{n}}{1},
Vn​(q)\displaystyle V_{n}(q) =−qn+1⟨n⟩q+qn+1+q2​n+1⟨n⟩q+q2​n+1⟨n⟩q+qn+1+−qn+11,\displaystyle=\frac{-q^{n+1}}{\langle n\rangle_{q}+q^{n+1}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{2n+1}}{\langle n\rangle_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{2n+1}}{\langle n\rangle_{q}+q^{n+1}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-q^{n+1}}{1},
Wn​(q)\displaystyle W_{n}(q) =𝒦i=0n−3⁡(qn−i[n−i]q−q+qn[i+2]q+qi+21−q)+q21.\displaystyle=\mathop{\vphantom{\sum}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{367007}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{262148}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}}\displaylimits_{i=0}^{n-3}\left(\frac{q^{n-i}}{[n-i]_{q}-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{n}}{[i+2]_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{i+2}}{1-q}\right)\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{2}}{1}.

When n=2n=2, we see that (1.20) coincides as expected with (1.18), provided we replace all 𝒦\mathcal{K} operators by 00. On the contrary, when n=1n=1 the HH-fraction expansion (1.17) of the qq-golden number Φ1\Phi_{1} is 33-periodic and does not fit into the above general formula.

Note also that an analogue of Theorem A exists for all shifts Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)} with ℓ=1,…,n+1\ell=1,\ldots,n+1 (see definition (1.2)), but will not be stated here for simplicity; see Theorem 7.3.

We continue the exposition of our main results and deal now with the Hankel determinants of Φn\Phi_{n}. First of all, as for the qq-golden number (1.12), all qq-metallic numbers Φn\Phi_{n} expand as Taylor series about zero: actually this is a general property of qq-deformations of positive real numbers, see [MGO22]. In particular, all their (ordinary or shifted) Hankel determinant sequences are well-defined. Thus, from now on we can fix a positive integer nn and set

Δj(ℓ):=Δj(ℓ)​(Φn)\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)}:=\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)}(\Phi_{n})

for short.

We begin with the generalization of (1.13).

Theorem B (Values and Periodicity).

Sequences Δ(ℓ)\Delta^{(\ell)} with ℓ∈{0,1,…,n+1}\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,n+1\} consist of −1,0,1-1,0,1 only. Moreover they are 2​n​(n+1)2n(n+1)-periodic when nn is even and 2​n​(n+1)2n(n+1)-antiperiodic (hence 4​n​(n+1)4n(n+1)-periodic) when nn is odd:

Δj+2​n​(n+1)(ℓ)=(−1)n​Δj(ℓ)for all ​j⩾0.\Delta_{j+2n(n+1)}^{(\ell)}=(-1)^{n}\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)}\quad\text{for all }j\geqslant 0.

This result reflects the periodicity of the HH-fraction expansion (1.20) but also reveals some symmetric patterns inside it; see Section 3.3. Explicit formulas for the Hankel determinants Δj(ℓ)\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)} will be given in Theorem 5.1 for the case ℓ=0\ell=0, together with a few examples for small values of nn; cases ℓ=1,…,n+1\ell=1,\ldots,n+1 will then follow from Theorem D below.

Now we describe the dynamics of the Hankel sequences:

Theorem C (Gale-Robinson recurrence).

Sequences Δ(ℓ)\Delta^{(\ell)} with ℓ∈{0,1,…,n+1}\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,n+1\} all satisfy the same following three-term Gale-Robinson recurrence:

Δj+2​n+2(ℓ)​Δj(ℓ)=Δj+2​n+1(ℓ)​Δj+1(ℓ)−(Δj+n+1(ℓ))2for all ​j⩾0.\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j+2n+2}\,\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j}=\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j+2n+1}\,\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j+1}-\bigl(\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j+n+1}\bigr)^{2}\quad\text{for all }j\geqslant 0.

Recall that a three-term Gale-Robinson sequence is a sequence (Sj)(S_{j}) defined by a recurrence of the form

(1.21) Sj​Sj+k=α​Sj+a​Sj+k−a+β​Sj+b​Sj+k−b,S_{j}S_{j+k}=\alpha S_{j+a}S_{j+k-a}+\beta S_{j+b}S_{j+k-b},

where k⩾4k\geqslant 4, 1⩽a<b⩽k/21\leqslant a<b\leqslant k/2 and α,β\alpha,\beta are some integer constants. Similarly, a four-term Gale-Robinson sequence is defined by allowing a third term γ​Sj+c​Sj+k−c\gamma S_{j+c}S_{j+k-c} in the right-hand side of (1.21); see [Gal91]. One can see at once that Somos-4 sequences and Somos-6 sequences (definition (1.16)) are special instances of three-term Gale-Robinson sequences and four-term Gale-Robinson sequences, respectively. Two such examples are thus provided by the Hankel determinants Δ(ℓ)​(Φn)\Delta^{(\ell)}(\Phi_{n}) (ℓ=0,1,…,n+1\ell=0,1,\ldots,n+1), for n=1n=1 (remind (1.15)) and n=2n=2 (see [OP25] §1.4).

While Somos sequences arose from elliptic function theory and can be studied from this point of view (see e.g. [Hon07, HS08]), some of their properties are best understood with S. Fomin & A. Zelevinsky’s theory of cluster algebras, and in particular the Laurent phenomenon [FZ02] which implies that all (three or four-term) Gale-Robinson sequences with positive integer coefficients α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma and initial data S0=S1=⋯=Sk−1=1S_{0}=S_{1}=\cdots=S_{k-1}=1 have the property of integrality, i.e. all terms of such a sequence are integers. This approach gave a unifying proof of the integrality of Somos-kk sequences for k=4,5,6,7k=4,5,6,7, which was already known to several authors.

Another main property of Somos-Gale-Robinson sequences is that they exhibit solutions to discrete dynamical systems which are integrable in the sense of Liouville-Arnold [FH14, HLK20]. In this way, Hankel determinants of qq-deformed metallic numbers provide examples of periodic {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\}-solutions of the corresponding discrete integrable systems; see the detailed example of Φ1​(q)\Phi_{1}(q) in [OP25], §1.4. Lastly, let us add that many examples of Somos sequences are produced by Hankel determinants, see [CHX15, Hon21] and the references therein.

Let us come back to the presentation of our results. As we have seen, Theorem C points out special relations existing between consecutive Hankel determinants inside the same ℓ\ell-shifted sequence. Incidentally, we have also discovered an explicit formula connecting the members of two consecutive shifted sequences, which implies in particular that all shifted sequences are completely determined by the ordinary Hankel determinant sequence Δ(0)=Δ⁡(Φn)\Delta^{(0)}=\Delta(\Phi_{n}):

Theorem D (Contiguity relations).

Pairs of consecutive shifted sequences (Δ(ℓ+1),Δ(ℓ))(\Delta^{(\ell+1)},\Delta^{(\ell)}) with ℓ∈{0,1,…,n}\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\} are interconnected by the following formula:

(1.22) Δj(ℓ+1)=(−1)j+n⁡(n+2​ℓ−1)2​Δj+n+1(ℓ)for all ​j⩾0.\Delta^{(\ell+1)}_{j}=(-1)^{j+\frac{n(n+2\ell-1)}{2}}\Delta^{(\ell)}_{j+n+1}\quad\text{for all }j\geqslant 0.

Note that Theorems B, C and D were proved by V. Ovsienko and the second author in [OP25] for n=1n=1 and n=2n=2 (see Theorem 1.6 and Theorem 1.8 therein), but only conjectured in the general case, excepting relation (1.22) which was proved when ℓ=n\ell=n for any nn (see Proposition 4.1 therein).

The reader has certainly noticed that all our statements deal with shifted sequences Δ(ℓ)\Delta^{(\ell)} for a parameter ℓ\ell such that 0⩽ℓ⩽n+10\leqslant\ell\leqslant n+1. As far as concerns the case ℓ⩾n+2\ell\geqslant n+2, computer experimentation incite us to formulate the following conjecture, that we are not able to prove so far, except for part (1) when n=1n=1, see Theorem 1.6 in [OP25].

Conjecture E.

The case ℓ⩾n+2\ell\geqslant n+2.

  1. 1)

    The sequence Δj(n+2)\Delta_{j}^{(n+2)} is 2​n​(n+1)2n(n+1)-periodic when nn is even and 2​n​(n+1)2n(n+1)-antiperiodic (hence 4​n​(n+1)4n(n+1)-periodic) when nn is odd, and consists of −2,−1,0,1,2-2,-1,0,1,2 only (except if n=1n=1: it can only take the values −1,0,1-1,0,1).

  2. 2)

    All sequences Δj(n+2)\Delta_{j}^{(n+2)} with ℓ⩾n+3\ell\geqslant n+3 are unbounded.

However, by looking at the functional equation satisfied by the shifted qq-metallic numbers Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)} and applying a result of [Han16], we show that weak versions of Theorem A and Theorem B hold, even in case ℓ⩾n+2\ell\geqslant n+2:

Theorem F (Periodicity modulo pp).

Let pp be a prime number. For any ℓ⩾0\ell\geqslant 0, the Hankel continued fraction of the shifted qq-metallic number Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)} and the corresponding Hankel determinants Δj(ℓ)\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)} (j⩾0j\geqslant 0) are ultimately periodic modulo pp.

Organization of the paper. Section 2 contains a brief presentation of S. Morier-Genoud and V. Ovsienko’s theory of qq-deformation of real numbers, applied in particular to metallic ratios. We recall also from [Han16] some fundamental results on Hankel continued fractions (alias HH-fractions), since it is the main tool we will use to compute Hankel determinants. We also explain how close Hankel continued fractions are to Artin’s regular continued fractions in the context of Laurent series.

In Section 3 we prove Theorem A i.e. the HH-fraction expansion of Φn\Phi_{n}. It will be obtained by using an algorithm well suited to power series that are solution of a quadratic equation with polynomial coefficients. This algorithm appeared first in the paper [Han16] and its application to our qq-metallic numbers Φn\Phi_{n} represents a quite technical work.

Theorems B and C will be obtained with the following strategy: instead of proving them directly for all values of the parameter ℓ\ell, we note that cases 1⩽ℓ⩽n+11\leqslant\ell\leqslant n+1 follow at once from the case ℓ=0\ell=0 and Theorem D. This is why Section 4 is devoted to the proof of Theorem B in the case ℓ=0\ell=0 only. The main tool here is the Hankel determinant formula for HH-fractions recalled in Section 2. It is worth noting that Theorem B will be established without calculating explicitly the Hankel determinants, since for showing periodicity and specifying the image set we need to understand more the pattern they form than their exact values.

Yet, computing the Hankel determinants Δj=Δj(0)​(Φn)\Delta_{j}=\Delta_{j}^{(0)}(\Phi_{n}) is inevitable for our other results and it is done in Section 5. We exploit the (anti-)periodicity shown by Theorem B together with some extra symmetry property to restrict ourselves to calculate the values of Δj\Delta_{j} only for a half-period (more or less), and we obtain explicit formulas similar to the ones in (1.14). They are presented in Theorem 5.1.

From these exact values of the Hankel determinants we then derive their Gale-Robinson dynamics and prove Theorem C in Section 6, still in the case ℓ=0\ell=0. This is an elementary but quite tedious task.

Finally, Section 7 is devoted to shifted Hankel determinants Δj(ℓ)\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)} with ℓ⩾1\ell\geqslant 1. We start by proving Theorem 7.3 which expresses the HH-fraction expansion of the shifted functions Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)} (1⩽ℓ⩽n+11\leqslant\ell\leqslant n+1) in terms of the one given in (1.20) for the initial function Φn=Φn(0)\Phi_{n}=\Phi_{n}^{(0)}. This result interconnects the HH-fractions expressions of all functions Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}, 0⩽ℓ⩽n+10\leqslant\ell\leqslant n+1 (see Corollary 7.5) and leads to the proof of Theorem D which, as noticed before, implies eventually the statements of Theorems B and C in the remaining cases 1⩽ℓ⩽n+11\leqslant\ell\leqslant n+1. In this section we also prove Theorem F.

Let us add a comment to our presentation. Although the cases of Φ1\Phi_{1} and Φ2\Phi_{2} were treated in [OP25] with much detail and very explicit formulas, they do not really represent the general case Φn\Phi_{n} which is more complex in nature. Moreover, our proofs are quite technical and lengthy. We thus think it is worthwhile to illustrate our present results on another concrete case, more representative of the general case but not too complicated either. We thus have chosen to focus on the case n=5n=5 throughout the paper to examplify the main results and the more technical proofs.

Note. Since all results stated in this article were proved in the cases n=1n=1 and n=2n=2 in [OP25], from now on it will be convenient to always assume that n⩾3n\geqslant 3, in order to avoid special discussions for the limit case n=2n=2 in some results.

Acknowledgements. We are grateful to Valentin Ovsienko for his stimulating interest and his useful comments on this work.

2. Background material

2.1. S. Morier-Genoud and V. Ovsienko’s qq-numbers

Our article is devoted to the continuous fraction expansion and Hankel determinant properties of the qq-deformation of particular real numbers. Let us define precisely what kind of quantization is meant here and give a brief introduction to the subject.

Quantization of integers is a very classical topic which goes back to Euler and Gauss: any integer n⩾0n\geqslant 0 can be deformed as a polynomial

(2.1) [n]q:=1−qn1−q=1+q+q2+⋯+qn−1.[n]_{q}:=\frac{1-q^{n}}{1-q}=1+q+q^{2}+\cdots+q^{n-1}.

Equivalently, one can define [n]q[n]_{q} as the unique solution of the recurrence

(2.2) [n+1]q=q​[n]q+1,[0]q=0.[n+1]_{q}=q[n]_{q}+1,\qquad[0]_{q}=0.

First form of definition (2.1) can also be used to define qq-deformation of negative integers n<0n<0:

[n]q:=1−qn1−q=−q−1−q−2−⋯−qn[n]_{q}:=\frac{1-q^{n}}{1-q}=-q^{-1}-q^{-2}-\cdots-q^{n}

and this gives a polynomial in q−1q^{-1}. A considerable amount of related objects have been based on definition (2.1), e.g. qq-factorials, qq-binomials, qq-hypergeometric functions, qq-calculus, etc. used in combinatorics, number theory, fractals, operator theory, mathematical physics… But until recently we missed a really satisfactory extension to more general numbers (reals, or even just rationals). For instance, for a rational m/nm/n, the naïve ideas

[mn]q:=[m]q[n]qor[mn]q:=1−qm/n1−q\left[\frac{m}{n}\right]_{q}:=\frac{[m]_{q}}{[n]_{q}}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\left[\frac{m}{n}\right]_{q}:=\frac{1-q^{m/n}}{1-q}

both lead to the same notion (up to a rescaling) which lacks crucial properties, such as verifying (2.2) or being a rational function of qq; it is then difficult to have nice enumerative or geometric interpretations.

In 2018, S. Morier-Genoud and V. Ovsienko began a beautiful construction of qq-analogues for rational, real and even complex numbers (see the seminal papers [MGO20, MGO22, Ovs21]) which in a very few years has shown to be successful in the mathematical community, thanks to connections with many topics: enumerative combinatorics, cluster algebras, Markov-Hurwitz approximation theory, braid groups, combinatorics of posets, Calabi-Yau triangulated categories, Lie algebras of differential operators, supersymmetry and supergeometry… see e.g. [MSS21, BBL23, CO23, KOR23, MO24, MGOV24, Tho24, KMR+25, Jou25].

Several equivalent models are available for Morier-Genoud & Ovsienko’s qq-real numbers. One of them involves continued fractions and is the best suited for our purposes.

Let x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} and consider its regular continued fraction expansion (finite if and only if x∈ℚx\in\mathbb{Q})

x=a0+1a1+1a2+1a3+⋯x\;=\;a_{0}+\frac{1}{a_{1}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{a_{2}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{a_{3}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}

with aia_{i} integers, positive for i⩾1i\geqslant 1. The qq-deformation or qq-analogue of xx is the following algebraic continued fraction:

(2.3) [x]q:=[a0]q+qa0[a1]q−1+q−a1[a2]q+qa2[a3]q−1+q−a3[a4]q+⋯[x]_{q}:=[a_{0}]_{q}+\frac{q^{a_{0}}}{[a_{1}]_{q^{-1}}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{-a_{1}}}{[a_{2}]_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{a_{2}}}{[a_{3}]_{q^{-1}}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{-a_{3}}}{[a_{4}]_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}

where [n]q[n]_{q} stands for the qq-integer as in (2.1), and [n]q−1=q1−n​[n]q[n]_{q^{-1}}=q^{1-n}[n]_{q} is the same expression with reciprocal parameter. Note that, when infinite, the right-hand side in (2.3) always converges in the sense of formal Laurent series.

Let us indicate some important characteristics of these qq-numbers; we cite the original references but most of the properties are explained also in the short survey [Ovs23].

  1. 1)

    [MGO20] For x∈ℤx\in\mathbb{Z}, [x]q[x]_{q} coincides with the classical definition (2.1) of Euler and Gauss.

  2. 2)

    [MGO22] For any x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, the Laurent series [x]q[x]_{q} has integer coefficients. More precisely the quantification map [⋅]q[\,\cdot\,]_{q} has the following images

    [⋅]q:ℚ⩾0→ℤ⩾0​(q),ℚ→ℤ⁡(q),ℝ⩾0→ℤ⁡[[q]],ℝ→ℤ⁡((q)).[\,\cdot\,]_{q}:\quad\mathbb{Q}_{\geqslant 0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}(q),\quad\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Z}(q),\quad\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}\to\mathbb{Z}[[q]],\quad\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{Z}(\!(q)\!).
  3. 3)

    [MGO22, LMG21] We have, for any x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R},

    [x+1]q=q​[x]q+1,[−1x]q=−1q​[x]q.[x+1]_{q}=q[x]_{q}+1,\qquad\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_{q}=-\frac{1}{q[x]_{q}}.

    These two crucial properties can be interpreted as commutation of the quantification map [⋅]q[\,\cdot\,]_{q} with the action on ℤ⁡((q))∪{∞}\mathbb{Z}(\!(q)\!)\cup\{\infty\} of a group of linear-fractional transformations which is isomorphic to the modular group PSL⁡(2,ℤ)\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{Z}). Moreover, [⋅]q[\,\cdot\,]_{q} is the unique PSL⁡(2,ℤ)\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb{Z})-invariant quantification which fixes 00; see [OP25], §2.2. Such an invariance is at the heart of the construction and plays a crucial role in the proof of numerous properties of these qq-numbers. Also, it can be understood as invariance with respect to the Burau representation of the braid group B3B_{3} [BBL23, MGOV24];

  4. 4)

    The radius of convergence of the Taylor series at 00 of the qq-golden number [1+52]q=Φ1​(q)\left[\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right]_{q}=\Phi_{1}(q) equals 3−52\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}, and it is conjectured that the radius of convergence of the Taylor series at 00 of the qq-deformation of any positive real number is always ⩾3−52\geqslant\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2} [LMGOV24]. This statement has already been verified for all qq-metallic numbers Φn​(q)\Phi_{n}(q) (see [Ren22, Ren23]) and for a large class of qq-deformed positive quadratic irrationals (see [Lec24], §4.4). For general rational or real numbers, progress has been made recently, see [EGMS24, Eti25].

  5. 5)

    [LMG21] When x=r±psx=\frac{r\pm\sqrt{p}}{s} is a quadratic irrational number (p,r,sp,r,s integers, p>0p>0), [x]q[x]_{q} is itself of the form

    (2.4) [x]q=R⁡(q)±P⁡(q)S⁡(q)[x]_{q}=\frac{R(q)\pm\sqrt{P(q)}}{S(q)}

    with P,R,Q∈ℤ⁡[q]P,R,Q\in\mathbb{Z}[q] and PP a palindrome.

Examples illustrating formula (2.4) are yielded by the qq-deformation Φn​(q)\Phi_{n}(q) of the metallic numbers ϕn=n+n2+42\phi_{n}=\frac{n+\sqrt{n^{2}+4}}{2}, n⩾1n\geqslant 1. Indeed, using definition (1.10) one can see that Φn\Phi_{n} is characterized by the functional equation

(2.5) q​Φn​(q)2+((1+qn)​(1−q)−q​[n]q)​Φn​(q)=1,q\,\Phi_{n}(q)^{2}+\left((1+q^{n})(1-q)-q\left[n\right]_{q}\right)\Phi_{n}(q)=1,

from which follows at once a formula of type (2.4):

Φn​(q)=12​q​(q​[n]q+(qn+1)​(q−1)+(q​[n]q+(qn+1)​(q−1))2+4​q).\Phi_{n}(q)=\frac{1}{2q}\left(q[n]_{q}+(q^{n}+1)(q-1)+\sqrt{\Bigl(q[n]_{q}+(q^{n}+1)(q-1)\Bigr)^{2}+4q}\right).

See [LMG21] or Proposition 2.5 in [OP25] for details. Another important property we will use is that Φn\Phi_{n} admits the following Taylor series expansion about zero:

(2.6) Φn​(q)=1+q+⋯+qn−1+q2​n+∑i=2​n+1+∞κi​qi,\Phi_{n}(q)=1+q+\cdots+q^{n-1}+q^{2n}+\sum_{i=2n+1}^{+\infty}\kappa_{i}q^{i},

where coefficients κi\kappa_{i} are integers; see Corollary 2.6 in [OP25].

2.2. HH-fractions and their Hankel determinants

In this subsection we recall some material from [Han16]. Fix a field 𝔽\mathbb{F}, an indeterminate qq, and let δ\delta be a positive integer. A super δ\delta-fraction is a continued fraction of the form

(2.7) F⁡(q)=v0​qk01+q​u1​(q)+−v1​qk0+k1+δ1+q​u2​(q)+−v2​qk1+k2+δ1+q​u3​(q)+−v3​qk2+k3+δ1+q​u4​(q)+⋯F(q)=\frac{v_{0}\,q^{k_{0}}}{1+qu_{1}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-v_{1}\,q^{k_{0}+k_{1}+\delta}}{1+qu_{2}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-v_{2}\,q^{k_{1}+k_{2}+\delta}}{1+qu_{3}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-v_{3}\,q^{k_{2}+k_{3}+\delta}}{1+qu_{4}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}

where vi∈𝔽∗v_{i}\in\mathbb{F}^{*}, ki∈ℤ⩾0k_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}, and ui∈𝔽⁡[q]u_{i}\in\mathbb{F}[q] are polynomials such that deg⁡(ui)⩽ki−1+δ−2\deg(u_{i})\leqslant k_{i-1}+\delta-2.

One of the main interests of this notion is that, not only (2.7) gives always a power series, but also, conversely, for a given positive integer δ\delta, any power series admits one and only one super δ\delta-fraction expansion (finite if and only if FF is rational). We will need to recall the proof of this result at the beginning of Section 3.1.

Example 2.2.

According to Theorem 3.2 in [OP25], for any n⩾1n\geqslant 1 the qq-deformed metallic number Φn\Phi_{n} admits the following 11-periodic expression as a super 33-fraction:

Φn​(q)=[n]q+q2​n⟨n⟩q+(q2​n+1⟨n⟩q+)∗\Phi_{n}(q)=[n]_{q}+\frac{q^{2n}}{\langle n\rangle_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\left(\frac{q^{2n+1}}{\langle n\rangle_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*}

where ⟨n⟩q\langle n\rangle_{q} was defined in (1.19). To be accurate, it is the shifted function

Φn(n+1)​(q)=Φn​(q)−[n]qqn+1\Phi_{n}^{(n+1)}(q)=\frac{\Phi_{n}(q)-[n]_{q}}{q^{n+1}}

(see definition (1.2)) which matches exactly definition (2.7) of a super 33-fraction, with kj≡n−1k_{j}\equiv n-1 for j⩾0j\geqslant 0, v0=1v_{0}=1 and vj≡−1v_{j}\equiv-1 for j⩾1j\geqslant 1.

Super δ\delta-fractions with δ=2\delta=2 are of special importance, they are called Hankel continued fractions, or more simply HH-fractions. Firstly, they generalize the classical notion of regular CC-fraction and regular JJ-fraction (when all kik_{i} are zero and δ=1\delta=1, δ=2\delta=2, respectively) and offer the possibility to compute the Hankel determinants of FF with the following striking formula (see Theorem 2.1 of [Han16]): if we define

(2.8) sp:=p+∑i=0p−1kiif ​p⩾1,s0:=0,𝒮:={sp,p⩾0}s_{p}:=p+\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}k_{i}\quad\text{if }p\geqslant 1,\quad s_{0}:=0,\quad\mathcal{S}:=\{s_{p},\ p\geqslant 0\}

and

(2.9) εp:=∑i=0p−1ki​(ki+1)2if ​p⩾1andε0:=0,\varepsilon_{p}:=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\frac{k_{i}\left(k_{i}+1\right)}{2}\quad\text{if }p\geqslant 1\quad\text{and}\quad\varepsilon_{0}:=0,

then

(2.10) {Δsp(F)=(−1)εpv0spv1sp−s1v2sp−s2⋯vp−1sp−sp−1if p⩾1,Δj​(F)=0if j∉𝒮.\begin{cases}\Delta_{s_{p}}(F)=(-1)^{\varepsilon_{p}}v_{0}^{s_{p}}v_{1}^{s_{p}-s_{1}}v_{2}^{s_{p}-s_{2}}\cdots v_{p-1}^{s_{p}-s_{p-1}}&if $p\geqslant 1$,\\ \Delta_{j}\left(F\right)=0&if $j\notin\mathcal{S}$.\end{cases}

(Recall that, by convention above, Δs0​(F)=Δ0​(F)=1\Delta_{s_{0}}(F)=\Delta_{0}(F)=1.) In this way, classical formulas known for CC-fractions and JJ-fractions (see e.g. Theorems 29 and 30 in [Kra05]) are generalized. Let us mention that similar formulas to (2.10) had been studied earlier in several references (mostly independently); see [Han20], the historical remark after Theorem 2.2.

Besides formula (2.10), a second reason for which we think that Hankel continued fractions have a particular interest is their strong connection with a classical continued fraction expansion in the field 𝔽⁡((q))\mathbb{F}(\!(q)\!) of Laurent series. Let us elaborate, since this relation was not yet discovered in the paper [Han16].

E. Artin has shown [Art24] that any Laurent series in qq

f⁡(q)=f−n​q−n+⋯+f−1​q−1+f0+f1​q+f2​q2+⋯f(q)=f_{-n}q^{-n}+\cdots+f_{-1}q^{-1}+f_{0}+f_{1}q+f_{2}q^{2}+\cdots

can be expanded, in a unique manner, as a continued fraction of the form

(2.11) f⁡(q)=a0​(1/q)+1a1​(1/q)+1a2​(1/q)+1a3​(1/q)+⋯f(q)=a_{0}(1/q)+\frac{1}{a_{1}(1/q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{a_{2}(1/q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{a_{3}(1/q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}

where a0a_{0} is a polynomial and, for any j⩾1j\geqslant 1, aja_{j} is a non constant polynomial. Artin’s expansion is traditionnaly called the regular continued fraction expansion of ff, because of the familiarity with the classical notion of regular continued fraction expansion for real numbers33 3 Usually, Artin’s theorem is stated in the field 𝔽⁡((1/q))\mathbb{F}(\!(1/q)\!) of Laurent series in the variable 1/q1/q but we adapt it to our context..

It turns out that regular continued fractions and Hankel continued fractions are closely and simply related when we restrict to power series. Take such a function

f⁡(q)=f1​q+f2​q2+f3​q3+⋯f(q)=f_{1}q+f_{2}q^{2}+f_{3}q^{3}+\cdots

with no constant term and write its regular expansion (2.11):

(2.12) f⁡(q)=1a1​(1/q)+1a2​(1/q)+1a3​(1/q)+⋯f(q)=\frac{1}{a_{1}(1/q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{a_{2}(1/q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{a_{3}(1/q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}

Fix j⩾1j\geqslant 1. Since aja_{j} is a non constant polynomial, there exist two natural numbers mjm_{j} and njn_{j}, with 1⩽nj⩽mj1\leqslant n_{j}\leqslant m_{j}, and a family of scalars (cj,r)r=njmj(c_{j,r})_{r=n_{j}}^{m_{j}}, with cj,nj≠0c_{j,n_{j}}\not=0 and cj,mj≠0c_{j,m_{j}}\not=0, such that

aj​(1/q)=cj,njqnj+cj,nj+1qnj+1+⋯+cj,mjqmj.a_{j}(1/q)=\frac{c_{j,n_{j}}}{q^{n_{j}}}+\frac{c_{j,n_{j}+1}}{q^{n_{j}+1}}+\cdots+\frac{c_{j,m_{j}}}{q^{m_{j}}}.

We then write

aj​(1/q)=(1+uj​(q)​q)​cj,mjqmja_{j}(1/q)=\bigl(1+u_{j}(q)q\bigr)\frac{c_{j,m_{j}}}{q^{m_{j}}}

where

uj​(q)=cj,njcj,mj​qmj−nj−1+cj,nj+1cj,mj​qmj−nj−2+⋯+cj,mj−1cj,mju_{j}(q)=\frac{c_{j,n_{j}}}{c_{j,m_{j}}}q^{m_{j}-n_{j}-1}+\frac{c_{j,n_{j}+1}}{c_{j,m_{j}}}{q^{m_{j}-n_{j}-2}}+\cdots+\frac{c_{j,m_{j}-1}}{c_{j,m_{j}}}

is a polynomial in qq satisfying

(2.13) deg⁡(uj)=mj−nj−1⩽mj−1.\deg(u_{j})=m_{j}-n_{j}-1\leqslant m_{j}-1.

But then (2.12) reads

f⁡(q)\displaystyle f(q) =1(1+u1​(q)​q)​c1,m1qm1+1(1+u2​(q)​q)​c2,m2qm2+1(1+u3​(q)​q)​c3,m3qm3+⋯\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(1+u_{1}(q)q)\frac{c_{1,m_{1}}}{q^{m_{1}}}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{(1+u_{2}(q)q)\frac{c_{2,m_{2}}}{q^{m_{2}}}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{(1+u_{3}(q)q)\frac{c_{3,m_{3}}}{q^{m_{3}}}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}
=c1,m1−1​qm11+u1​(q)​q+c1,m1−1​c2,m2−1​qm1+m21+u2​(q)​q+c2,m2−1​c3,m3−1​qm2+m31+u3​(q)​q+⋯\displaystyle=\frac{c_{1,m_{1}}^{-1}{q^{m_{1}}}}{1+u_{1}(q)q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{c_{1,m_{1}}^{-1}c_{2,m_{2}}^{-1}{q^{m_{1}+m_{2}}}}{1+u_{2}(q)q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{c_{2,m_{2}}^{-1}c_{3,m_{3}}^{-1}{q^{m_{2}+m_{3}}}}{1+u_{3}(q)q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}

This expression is exactly of the form

f⁡(q)=q​F​(q)f(q)=q\,F(q)

where

F⁡(q)=v0​qk01+q​u1​(q)+−v1​qk0+k1+21+q​u2​(q)+−v2​qk1+k2+21+q​u3​(q)+⋯F(q)=\frac{v_{0}\,q^{k_{0}}}{1+qu_{1}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-v_{1}\,q^{k_{0}+k_{1}+2}}{1+qu_{2}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-v_{2}\,q^{k_{1}+k_{2}+2}}{1+qu_{3}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}

and

(2.14) {v0=c1,m1−1vj=−(cj,mj​cj+1,mj+1)−1for j⩾1kj=mj+1−1for j⩾0.\begin{cases}v_{0}=c_{1,m_{1}}^{-1}&\\ v_{j}=-\left(c_{j,m_{j}}c_{j+1,m_{j+1}}\right)^{-1}&for $j\geqslant 1$\\ k_{j}=m_{j+1}-1&for $j\geqslant 0$.\end{cases}

Since deg⁡(uj)⩽kj−1\deg(u_{j})\leqslant k_{j-1} by (2.13), the expression of F⁡(q)F(q) above is a HH-fraction expansion (take (2.7) with δ=2\delta=2) for the parameters (2.14).

In conclusion, Artin’s regular continued fraction expansion for the power series without constant term f⁡(q)f(q) yields a Hankel continued fraction expansion for the power series F⁡(q)=f⁡(q)/qF(q)=f(q)/q. And conversely, the Hankel continued fraction expansion for any power series g⁡(q)g(q) yields the regular continued fraction expansion for (g⁡(q)−g⁡(0))/q(g(q)-g(0))/q. We thus have a correspondance between the two kinds of expansion and it is easy to switch from one model to the other, thanks to the conversion formulas (2.14).

As an example, consider a regular JJ-fraction expansion

F⁡(q)=v01+u1​q+−v1​q21+u2​q+−v2​q21+u3​q+⋯F(q)=\frac{v_{0}}{1+u_{1}q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-v_{1}\,q^{2}}{1+u_{2}q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-v_{2}\,q^{2}}{1+u_{3}q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}

where ui,viu_{i},v_{i} are scalars and viv_{i} are nonzero. It is nothing but a HH-fraction with all kj=0k_{j}=0, and if

f⁡(q)=f0+q​F​(q),f(q)=f_{0}+qF(q),

then f⁡(q)f(q) admits a regular continued fraction (2.12) with all aja_{j} polynomials of degree 11 and determined by the parameters of the JJ-fraction as follows:

f⁡(q)=f0+1c1+d1q+1c2+d2q+1c3+d3q+⋯f(q)=f_{0}+\frac{1}{c_{1}+\frac{d_{1}}{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{c_{2}+\frac{d_{2}}{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{1}{c_{3}+\frac{d_{3}}{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}

with

{dj≠0for j⩾0v0=d1−1vj=−(dj​dj+1)−1for j⩾1uj=cj/djfor j⩾0.\begin{cases}d_{j}\neq 0&for $j\geqslant 0$\\ v_{0}=d_{1}^{-1}&\\ v_{j}=-(d_{j}d_{j+1})^{-1}&for $j\geqslant 1$\\ u_{j}=c_{j}/d_{j}&for $j\geqslant 0$.\end{cases}

Such a transformation for regular JJ-fractions may be considered as folklore and not necessarily connected to Artin’s expansion; it appears e.g. in [Wal48], §42.

3. The Hankel continued fraction expansion for Φn\Phi_{n}

We already recalled the examples of HH-fractions (1.17) and (1.18) that were obtained for Φ1​(q)\Phi_{1}(q) and Φ2​(q)\Phi_{2}(q) in [OP25]. In this section we prove that the HH-fraction presentation for Φn\Phi_{n} stated in Theorem A is actually valid for all n⩾3n\geqslant 3. It is a quite difficult problem, and we will solve it by applying a variant of an algorithm which was introduced in [Han16]. It was originally designed to treat quadratic power series in coefficients in a finite field, but actually works perfectly for any field 𝔽\mathbb{F} and in particular in our situation 𝔽=ℚ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{Q}.

3.1. An algorithm for HH-fractions

Let 𝔽\mathbb{F} be a field, qq an indeterminate. Here we present an algorithm which is tailored to produce explicit HH-fractions for a certain class of power series F∈𝔽⁡[[q]]F\in\mathbb{F}[[q]], including our particular function Φn∈ℚ⁡[[q]]\Phi_{n}\in\mathbb{Q}[[q]].

To begin with, let us explain how any power series F∈𝔽⁡[[q]]F\in\mathbb{F}[[q]] can we written, in a unique way, as a HH-fraction, i.e. a super δ\delta-fraction (2.7) with δ=2\delta=2 (actually the same argument works for any δ\delta, see the proof of Theorem 2.1 in [Han16]).

First, one roughly expands the power series F⁡(q)F(q) as

F⁡(q)=v0​qk0+O⁡(qk0+1)F(q)=v_{0}q^{k_{0}}+O(q^{k_{0}+1})

where v0≠0v_{0}\neq 0 and k0∈ℤ⩾0k_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}, so that F⁡(q)/(v0​qk0)=1+O⁡(q)F(q)/(v_{0}q^{k_{0}})=1+O(q). Hence one can write

(3.1) v0​qk0F⁡(q)=D0​(q)−qk0+2​F1​(q)\frac{v_{0}q^{k_{0}}}{F(q)}=D_{0}(q)-q^{k_{0}+2}F_{1}(q)

with D0D_{0} a polynomial such that D0​(0)=1D_{0}(0)=1 and deg⁡(D0)⩽k0+1\deg(D_{0})\leqslant k_{0}+1, and F1​(q)F_{1}(q) a power series. Notice that the condition on the degree makes D0D_{0} and F1F_{1} uniquely defined. Equivalently we have

(3.2) F⁡(q)=v0​qk0D0​(q)−qk0+2​F1​(q)F(q)=\frac{v_{0}q^{k_{0}}}{D_{0}(q)-q^{k_{0}+2}F_{1}(q)}

and repeating the process with F1F_{1} will give similar objects v1,k1,D1,F2v_{1},k_{1},D_{1},F_{2} such that

F1​(q)=v1​qk1D1​(q)−qk1+2​F2​(q)F_{1}(q)=\frac{v_{1}q^{k_{1}}}{D_{1}(q)-q^{k_{1}+2}F_{2}(q)}

hence

F⁡(q)=v0​qk0D0​(q)+−v1​qk0+k1+2D1​(q)−qk1+2​F2​(q).F(q)=\frac{v_{0}q^{k_{0}}}{D_{0}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-v_{1}q^{k_{0}+k_{1}+2}}{D_{1}(q)-q^{k_{1}+2}F_{2}(q)}.

Going on with this process inductively will lead to the Hankel continued fraction

(3.3) F⁡(q)=v0​qk0D0​(q)+−v1​qk0+k1+2D1​(q)+−v2​qk1+k2+2D2​(q)+⋯F(q)=\frac{v_{0}q^{k_{0}}}{D_{0}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-v_{1}q^{k_{0}+k_{1}+2}}{D_{1}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-v_{2}q^{k_{1}+k_{2}+2}}{D_{2}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathord{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$\cdots$}}

Thus we have proved that any power series F⁡(q)F(q) can be developed (uniquely) as a HH-fraction, and next problem is to compute explicitly data sequences (vi)(v_{i}), (ki)(k_{i}) and (Di)(D_{i}) from FF. We do not know the answer in general, but when the power series is quadratic in the sense that there exists three polynomials A,B,C∈𝔽⁡[q]A,B,C\in\mathbb{F}[q] such that

(3.4) A+B​F+C​F2=0A+BF+CF^{2}=0

(together with some conditions on A,B,CA,B,C that will be described soon) an algorithm will help us to do that. Of course, it will only be usable in case of a finite number of steps. This situation can happen when sequences of data are finite by nature (e.g. when the field is finite; see the original applications in [Han16]) or when the super fraction is going to be periodic (or ultimately periodic), which will be our case when considering F=ΦnF=\Phi_{n}, although the field 𝔽=ℚ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{Q} is infinite.

Let us elaborate. Suppose from now on that FF satisfies the quadratic equation (3.4) together with the following conditions

(3.5) A≠0,B⁡(0)=1,C≠0,C⁡(0)=0.A\neq 0,\quad B(0)=1,\quad C\neq 0,\quad C(0)=0.

(Recall from (2.5) that this is the case for F=ΦnF=\Phi_{n}.) Then the quadratic equation (3.4) with conditions (3.5) has a unique solution

F=−B+B2−4​A​C2​C.F=\frac{-B+\sqrt{B^{2}-4AC}}{2C}.

According to (3.1) we need to know the first term of the expansion of F⁡(q)F(q) about q=0q=0. Because

F⁡(q)=−A⁡(q)B⁡(q)+C⁡(q)​F​(q)F(q)=\frac{-A(q)}{B(q)+C(q)F(q)}

with conditions (3.5), we see that this amounts to know the lower degree term of A⁡(q)A(q). Writing the nonzero polynomial AA as

(3.6) A⁡(q)=ak​qk+O⁡(qk+1)A(q)=a_{k}q^{k}+O(q^{k+1})

with k∈ℤ⩾0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0} and ak≠0a_{k}\not=0, the left-hand side of (3.1) reads

−ak​qkF⁡(q)\displaystyle\frac{-a_{k}q^{k}}{F(q)} =−2​ak​qk​C−B+B2−4​A​C\displaystyle=\frac{-2a_{k}q^{k}C}{-B+\sqrt{B^{2}-4AC}}
=−2​ak​qk​C​(B2−4​A​C+B)−4​A​C\displaystyle=\frac{-2a_{k}q^{k}C(\sqrt{B^{2}-4AC}+B)}{-4AC}
(3.7) =−ak​qk​CA×−B−B2−4​A​C2​C.\displaystyle=\frac{-a_{k}q^{k}C}{A}\times\frac{-B-\sqrt{B^{2}-4AC}}{2C}.

(From now on, for polynomials we will often write PP instead of P⁡(q)P(q), for easier reading.) Let

Γ⁡(q)=∑j=0+∞γj​qj=1−1−4​q2​q\Gamma(q)=\sum_{j=0}^{+\infty}\gamma_{j}q^{j}=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4q}}{2q}

be the generating function of the Catalan numbers (1.3). We calculate

Γ⁡(A​CB2)=BA×B−B2−4​A​C2​C\Gamma\left(\frac{AC}{B^{2}}\right)=\frac{B}{A}\times\frac{B-\sqrt{B^{2}-4AC}}{2C}

which implies

−B−B2−4​A​C2​C\displaystyle\frac{-B-\sqrt{B^{2}-4AC}}{2C} =−BC−−B+B2−4​A​C2​C\displaystyle=-\frac{B}{C}-\frac{-B+\sqrt{B^{2}-4AC}}{2C}
=−BC+AB​Γ​(A​CB2)\displaystyle=-\frac{B}{C}+\frac{A}{B}\>\Gamma\left(\frac{AC}{B^{2}}\right)
=−BC+AB​∑j=0+∞γj​(A​CB2)j.\displaystyle=-\frac{B}{C}+\frac{A}{B}\sum_{j=0}^{+\infty}\gamma_{j}\left(\frac{AC}{B^{2}}\right)^{j}.

Inserting this equality in (3.7) we deduce that

−ak​qkF⁡(q)\displaystyle\frac{-a_{k}q^{k}}{F(q)} =−ak​qk​CA​(−BC+AB​∑j=0+∞γj​(A​CB2)j)\displaystyle=\frac{-a_{k}q^{k}C}{A}\biggl(-\frac{B}{C}+\frac{A}{B}\sum_{j=0}^{+\infty}\gamma_{j}\left(\frac{AC}{B^{2}}\right)^{j}\biggr)
=−ak​qk​BA​(−1+∑j=0+∞γj​(A​CB2)j+1).\displaystyle=\frac{-a_{k}q^{k}B}{A}\biggl(-1+\sum_{j=0}^{+\infty}\gamma_{j}\left(\frac{AC}{B^{2}}\right)^{j+1}\biggr).

Now, as explained in (3.1) there exists a unique polynomial DD with D⁡(0)=1D(0)=1 and deg⁡(D)⩽k+1\deg(D)\leqslant k+1, and a unique power series R1R_{1} such that

−ak​qkF⁡(q)=D−qk+2​R1​(q)\frac{-a_{k}q^{k}}{F(q)}=D-q^{k+2}R_{1}(q)

hence

(3.8) −ak​qk​BA​(−1+∑j=0+∞γj​(A​CB2)j+1)=D⁡(q)−qk+2​R1​(q).\frac{-a_{k}q^{k}B}{A}\biggl(-1+\sum_{j=0}^{+\infty}\gamma_{j}\left(\frac{AC}{B^{2}}\right)^{j+1}\biggr)=D(q)-q^{k+2}R_{1}(q).

Recall that we want to compute explicitly the polynomial DD since it will produce the denominator in the first step (3.2) of the HH-fraction expansion of FF. To do so, remind from (3.5) that we have B=1+O⁡(q)B=1+O(q) and C=O⁡(q)C=O(q). Together with (3.6) this implies

A​CB2=[ak​qk+O⁡(qk+1)]⋅O⁡(q)[1+O⁡(q)]2=ak​O​(qk+1)+O⁡(qk+2)\frac{AC}{B^{2}}=\frac{[a_{k}q^{k}+O(q^{k+1})]\cdot O(q)}{[1+O(q)]^{2}}=a_{k}O(q^{k+1})+O(q^{k+2})

so that (A​CB2)j+1=O⁡(qk+2)\left(\frac{AC}{B^{2}}\right)^{j+1}=O(q^{k+2}) for all j⩾1j\geqslant 1. In other words the series in the left-hand side of (3.8) can contribute to DD only with its first term, and there exists a power series R2R_{2} such that

−ak​qk​BA​(−1+A​CB2)=D−qk+2​R2​(q).\frac{-a_{k}q^{k}B}{A}\left(-1+\frac{AC}{B^{2}}\right)=D-q^{k+2}R_{2}(q).

Writing C⁡(q)=c1​q+c2​q2+⋯+cd​qdC(q)=c_{1}q+c_{2}q^{2}+\cdots+c_{d}q^{d} and remembering B=1+O⁡(q)B=1+O(q), we conclude that DD is uniquely determined by the following conditions:

(3.9) deg⁡(D)⩽k+1andak​qk​BA−ak​c1​qk+1=D−qk+2​R3​(q)\deg(D)\leqslant k+1\quad\text{and}\quad a_{k}q^{k}\frac{B}{A}-a_{k}c_{1}q^{k+1}=D-q^{k+2}R_{3}(q)

for some power series R3R_{3}. Property that D⁡(0)=1D(0)=1 will be automatic, by (3.1).

All of this leads us to formulate the following definition, already introduced in [Han16], but refined here in the special case δ=2\delta=2, i.e. when super fractions are HH-fractions.

Algorithm 3.1.

[Algorithm NextABC for HH-fractions]

Prototype:

(A∗,B∗,C∗,k,ak,D)=𝙽𝚎𝚡𝚝𝙰𝙱𝙲⁡(A,B,C)(A^{*},B^{*},C^{*},k,a_{k},D)={\tt NextABC}(A,B,C).

Input:

three polynomials A,B,C∈𝔽⁡[q]A,B,C\in\mathbb{F}[q] satisfying (3.5).

Output:

a positive integer kk,
a nonzero scalar ak∈𝔽a_{k}\in\mathbb{F},
a polynomial D∈𝔽⁡[q]D\in\mathbb{F}[q] of degree ⩽k+1\leqslant k+1 such that D⁡(0)=1D(0)=1,
three polynomials A∗,B∗,C∗∈𝔽⁡[q]A^{*},B^{*},C^{*}\in\mathbb{F}[q] satisfying (3.5).

Step 1:

Define k,akk,a_{k} by (3.6).

Step 2:

Define DD by (3.9).

Step 3:

Set

A∗\displaystyle{A^{*}} :=1q2​k+2​(−D2​Aak+B​D​qk−C​ak​q2​k)\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{q^{2k+2}}\left(\frac{-D^{2}A}{a_{k}}+BDq^{k}-Ca_{k}q^{2k}\right)
B∗\displaystyle{B^{*}} :=2​A​Dak​qk−B\displaystyle:=\frac{2AD}{a_{k}q^{k}}-B
C∗\displaystyle{C^{*}} :=−A​q2ak.\displaystyle:=-\frac{Aq^{2}}{a_{k}}.

In this algorithm, all objects are well (and uniquely) defined by the previous discussion. It remains only to justify that A∗,B∗,C∗A^{*},B^{*},C^{*} are indeed polynomials and that they also satisfy (3.5); but this comes from Lemma 3.2 in [Han16].

Now, let us check that our algorithm NextABC works as expected:

  • ∙\bullet

    Start with a quadratic power series FF as in (3.4), with the associated triple of polynomials (A,B,C)(A,B,C) satisfying (3.5).

  • ∙\bullet

    Set (A1,B1,C1,k0,a0,D0):=𝙽𝚎𝚡𝚝𝙰𝙱𝙲⁡(A,B,C)(A_{1},B_{1},C_{1},k_{0},a_{0},D_{0}):={\tt NextABC}(A,B,C). Then we have

    F⁡(q)=−a0​qk0D0​(q)−qk0+2​F1​(q)F(q)=\frac{-a_{0}q^{k_{0}}}{D_{0}(q)-q^{k_{0}+2}F_{1}(q)}

    as in (3.2). The main point now is that the power series F1F_{1} is itself quadratic, more precisely it satisfies the equation

    A1+B1​F1+C1​F12=0.A_{1}+B_{1}F_{1}+C_{1}F_{1}^{2}=0.

    This fact is also a statement taken from Lemma 3.2 in [Han16].

  • ∙\bullet

    Thus the algorithm can be applied a second time and we set (A2,B2,C2,k1,a1,D1):=𝙽𝚎𝚡𝚝𝙰𝙱𝙲⁡(A1,B1,C1)(A_{2},B_{2},C_{2},k_{1},a_{1},D_{1}):={\tt NextABC}(A_{1},B_{1},C_{1}). As in the beginning of this subsection we have

    F1​(q)=−a1​qk1D1​(q)−qk1+2​F2​(q)henceF⁡(q)=−a0​qk0D0​(q)+a1​qk0+k1+2D1​(q)−qk1+2​F2​(q)F_{1}(q)=\frac{-a_{1}q^{k_{1}}}{D_{1}(q)-q^{k_{1}+2}F_{2}(q)}\qquad\text{hence}\qquad F(q)=\frac{-a_{0}q^{k_{0}}}{D_{0}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{a_{1}q^{k_{0}+k_{1}+2}}{D_{1}(q)-q^{k_{1}+2}F_{2}(q)}

    with F2F_{2} still quadratic: A2+B2​F2+C2​F22=0A_{2}+B_{2}F_{2}+C_{2}F_{2}^{2}=0. Going on through this process will define (kj,aj,Dj)(k_{j},a_{j},D_{j}) for any j⩾0j\geqslant 0 and will lead to the aimed HH-fraction (3.3).

  • ∙\bullet

    Suppose that there exists integers 0<p<p′0<p<p^{\prime} such that (Ap′,Bp′,Cp′)=(Ap,Bp,Cp)(A_{p^{\prime}},B_{p^{\prime}},C_{p^{\prime}})=(A_{p},B_{p},C_{p}). Then the algorithm will repeat the same sequences indefinitely and the HH-fraction is ultimately periodic:

    (3.10) F⁡(q)=−a0​qk0D0​(q)+𝒦j=1p−1⁡aj​qkj−1+kj+2Dj​(q)+(𝒦j=pp′−1⁡aj​qkj−1+kj+2Dj​(q))∗.F(q)=\frac{-a_{0}q^{k_{0}}}{D_{0}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathop{\vphantom{\sum}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{367007}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{262148}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}}\displaylimits_{j=1}^{p-1}\frac{a_{j}q^{k_{j-1}+k_{j}+2}}{D_{j}(q)}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\left(\mathop{\vphantom{\sum}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{367007}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{262148}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}}\displaylimits_{j=p}^{p^{\prime}-1}\frac{a_{j}q^{k_{j-1}+k_{j}+2}}{D_{j}(q)}\right)^{*}.

    This is precisely what is going to happen when F=ΦnF=\Phi_{n}.

Of course, in theory it is not necessary to define DD by (3.9) rather than by (3.1) to get the HH-fraction; the original algorithm in [Han16], constructed to produce super δ\delta-fractions for any δ\delta, does not do that. But in our case δ=2\delta=2, it will be much more easier to find the polynomials DjD_{j} by looking at simple expressions involving only polynomials Aj,Bj,CjA_{j},B_{j},C_{j}.

Remark 3.2.

Actually, Algorithm 3.1 can be simplified. Indeed, because of definition of C∗C^{*} in Step 3 we see that we will always have C=O⁡(q2)C=O(q^{2}), except maybe at first implementation of the algorithm. In other words c1=0c_{1}=0 and definition (3.9) of the polynomial DD in Step 2 of Algorithm 3.1 becomes simpler.
Actually, we will encounter further simplifications when applying Algorithm 3.1 to F=ΦnF=\Phi_{n}: the coefficients aka_{k} will always be ±1\pm 1, as we shall see soon.

3.2. Proof of Theorem A

Fix an integer n⩾3n\geqslant 3. In this subsection we will apply Algorithm 3.1 to F=ΦnF=\Phi_{n} and prove Theorem A. As explained after the statement of Algorithm 3.1, our task is to exhibit a family of sextuplets associated with F=ΦnF=\Phi_{n}:

(3.11) 𝒬j:=(Aj,Bj,Cj,kj,aj,Dj),j⩾0,\mathcal{Q}_{j}:=(A_{j},B_{j},C_{j},k_{j},a_{j},D_{j}),\quad j\geqslant 0,

by applying repeatedly the algorithm, until periodicity is observed and stops the process. Then the HH-fraction will have the form (3.10).

In fact, it turns out that we will need to define two different families of objects to achieve our goal. We start with the first one.

Definition 3.3.

Let (𝒬1(m))m⩾1\bigl(\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{(m)}\bigr)_{m\geqslant 1} denote the sequence of sextuplets

𝒬1(m)=(A1(m),B1(m),C1(m),k1(m),ak1(m),D1(m))\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{(m)}=\bigl(A_{1}^{(m)},B_{1}^{(m)},C_{1}^{(m)},k_{1}^{(m)},a_{k_{1}}^{(m)},D_{1}^{(m)}\bigr)

constituted of polynomials A1(m),B1(m),C1(m),D1(m)A_{1}^{(m)},B_{1}^{(m)},C_{1}^{(m)},D_{1}^{(m)}, integers k1(m)k_{1}^{(m)} and numbers ak1(m)∈{±1}a_{k_{1}}^{(m)}\in\{\pm 1\} defined as follows:

    A1(m)\displaystyle A_{1}^{(m)} =−1,\displaystyle=-1, B1(m)\displaystyle B_{1}^{(m)} =−(q2−q+1)​(qn+1)−2​qq−1,\displaystyle=-\frac{{\left(q^{2}-q+1\right)}{\left(q^{n}+1\right)}-2\,q}{q-1}, C1(m)\displaystyle C_{1}^{(m)} =q,\displaystyle=q,
    k1(m)\displaystyle k_{1}^{(m)} =0,\displaystyle=0, ak1(m)\displaystyle a_{k_{1}}^{(m)} =−1,\displaystyle=-1, D1(m)\displaystyle D_{1}^{(m)} =1−q.\displaystyle=1-q.
  2. 2)

    If m=3​j+1m=3j+1 with 1⩽j⩽n−21\leqslant j\leqslant n-2:

    A1(m)\displaystyle A_{1}^{(m)} =−(q2−q+1)​(qn−j−qn−1)+qj+1(q−1)2,\displaystyle=-\frac{{\left(q^{2}-q+1\right)}{\left(q^{n-j}-q^{n}-1\right)}+q^{j+1}}{{\left(q-1\right)}^{2}}, B1(m)\displaystyle B_{1}^{(m)} =−(q2−q+1)​(qn+1)−2​qj+1q−1,\displaystyle=-\frac{{\left(q^{2}-q+1\right)}{\left(q^{n}+1\right)}-2\,q^{j+1}}{q-1},
    C1(m)\displaystyle C_{1}^{(m)} =−qj+1,\displaystyle=-q^{j+1}, k1(m)\displaystyle k_{1}^{(m)} =0,\displaystyle=0,
    ak1(m)\displaystyle a_{k_{1}}^{(m)} =1,\displaystyle=1, D1(m)\displaystyle D_{1}^{(m)} =1−q.\displaystyle=1-q.
  3. 3)

    If m=3​j+2m=3j+2 with 0⩽j⩽n−20\leqslant j\leqslant n-2:

    A1(m)\displaystyle A_{1}^{(m)} =(q2−q+1)​qn−j−2,\displaystyle={\left(q^{2}-q+1\right)}q^{n-j-2}, B1(m)\displaystyle B_{1}^{(m)} =(q2−q+1)​(2​qn−j−qn−1)q−1,\displaystyle=\frac{{\left(q^{2}-q+1\right)}{\left(2\,q^{n-j}-q^{n}-1\right)}}{q-1},
    C1(m)\displaystyle C_{1}^{(m)} =(q4−q3+q2)​(qn−j−qn−1)+qj+3(q−1)2,\displaystyle=\frac{{\left(q^{4}-q^{3}+q^{2}\right)}{\left(q^{n-j}-q^{n}-1\right)}+q^{j+3}}{{\left(q-1\right)}^{2}}, k1(m)\displaystyle k_{1}^{(m)} =n−2−j,\displaystyle=n-2-j,
    ak1(m)\displaystyle a_{k_{1}}^{(m)} =1,\displaystyle=1, D1(m)\displaystyle D_{1}^{(m)} =qn−j−1q−1=[n−j]q.\displaystyle=\frac{q^{n-j}-1}{q-1}=[n-j]_{q}.
  4. 4)

    If m=3​j+3m=3j+3 with 0⩽j⩽n−20\leqslant j\leqslant n-2:

    A1(m)\displaystyle A_{1}^{(m)} =qj,\displaystyle=q^{j}, B1(m)\displaystyle B_{1}^{(m)} =(q2−q+1)​[n]q,\displaystyle=\left(q^{2}-q+1\right)[n]_{q}, C1(m)\displaystyle C_{1}^{(m)} =−(q2−q+1)​qn−j,\displaystyle=-{\left(q^{2}-q+1\right)}q^{n-j},
    k1(m)\displaystyle k_{1}^{(m)} =j,\displaystyle=j, ak1(m)\displaystyle a_{k_{1}}^{(m)} =1,\displaystyle=1, D1(m)\displaystyle D_{1}^{(m)} =[j+2]q−q.\displaystyle=[j+2]_{q}-q.

Using (2.5) we see that definition of (A1(1),B1(1),C1(1))\bigl(A_{1}^{(1)},B_{1}^{(1)},C_{1}^{(1)}\bigr) is such that

A1(1)+B1(1)​Φn+C1(1)​Φn2=0,A_{1}^{(1)}+B_{1}^{(1)}\Phi_{n}+C_{1}^{(1)}\Phi_{n}^{2}=0,

i.e. this first triple corresponds to the initialization of the process described in Section 3.1. Now we prove that our algorithm NextABC produces successively all the sequences defined above.

Lemma 3.4.

Suppose that 1⩽m⩽3​n−31\leqslant m\leqslant 3n-3. Then

𝙽𝚎𝚡𝚝𝙰𝙱𝙲⁡(A1(m),B1(m),C1(m))=(A1(m+1),B1(m+1),C1(m+1),k1(m),ak1(m),D1(m)).{\tt NextABC}\bigl(A_{1}^{(m)},B_{1}^{(m)},C_{1}^{(m)}\bigr)=\bigl(A_{1}^{(m+1)},B_{1}^{(m+1)},C_{1}^{(m+1)},k_{1}^{(m)},a_{k_{1}}^{(m)},D_{1}^{(m)}\bigr).
Proof.

Let mm be an integer such that 1⩽m⩽3​n−31\leqslant m\leqslant 3n-3. To make our calculations easier to read, we just write AA, BB, CC, kk, aka_{k}, DD instead of A1(m)A_{1}^{(m)}, B1(m)B_{1}^{(m)}, C1(m)C_{1}^{(m)}, k1(m)k_{1}^{(m)}, ak1(m)a_{k_{1}}^{(m)}, D1(m)D_{1}^{(m)} respectively. Let us apply the algorithm NextABC for each case introduced in Definition 3.3.

  1. 1)

    Case m=1m=1.

    Step 1:

    Since A=−1A=-1, (3.6) gives k=0k=0 and ak=−1a_{k}=-1.

    Step 2:

    Since C=qC=q, we have c1=1c_{1}=1 and (3.9) says that the polynomial DD is defined by

    q−(q2−q+1)​(qn+1)−2​qq−1=1−qn+1−qn−qq−1=D+O⁡(q2)q-\frac{{\left(q^{2}-q+1\right)}{\left(q^{n}+1\right)}-2\,q}{q-1}=1-q^{n+1}-\frac{q^{n}-q}{q-1}=D+O(q^{2})

    and that deg⁡(D)⩽1\deg(D)\leqslant 1. We see immediately that D=1−qD=1-q.

    Step 3:

    Applying the definitions, we easily check that A∗=A(2)A^{*}=A^{(2)}, B∗=B(2)B^{*}=B^{(2)}, C∗=C(2)C^{*}=C^{(2)}.

  2. 2)

    Case m=3​j+1m=3j+1 with 1⩽j⩽n−21\leqslant j\leqslant n-2.

    Step 1:

    Here,

    A=−(q2−q+1)​(qn−j−qn−1)+qj+1(q−1)2=1+O⁡(q)A=-\frac{{\left(q^{2}-q+1\right)}{\left(q^{n-j}-q^{n}-1\right)}+q^{j+1}}{{\left(q-1\right)}^{2}}=1+O(q)

    so that k=0k=0 and ak=1a_{k}=1.

    Step 2:

    Since C=−qj+1C=-q^{j+1}, we have c1=0c_{1}=0 and by (3.9), DD is the unique polynomial of degree ⩽1\leqslant 1 such that

    BA=D+O⁡(q2).\frac{B}{A}=D+O(q^{2}).

    But

    BA=((q2−q+1)​(qn+1)−2​qj+1)​(q−1)(q2−q+1)​(qn−j−qn−1)+qj+1=−1+2​q+O⁡(q2)−1+q+O⁡(q2)\frac{B}{A}=\frac{{(\left(q^{2}-q+1)(q^{n}+1)-2\,q^{j+1}\right)}{(q-1)}}{{(q^{2}-q+1)}{(q^{n-j}-q^{n}-1)}+q^{j+1}}=\frac{-1+2q+O(q^{2})}{-1+q+O(q^{2})}

    because 1⩽j⩽n−21\leqslant j\leqslant n-2, hence D=1−qD=1-q.

    Step 3:

    We obtain easily A∗=A(m+1),B∗=B(m+1),C∗=C(m+1)A^{*}=A^{(m+1)},\ B^{*}=B^{(m+1)},\ C^{*}=C^{(m+1)}.

  3. 3)

    Case m=3​j+2m=3j+2 with 0⩽j⩽n−20\leqslant j\leqslant n-2.

    Step 1:

    Since A=(q2−q+1)​qn−j−2=qn−j−2+O⁡(qn−j−1)A={\left(q^{2}-q+1\right)}q^{n-j-2}=q^{n-j-2}+O(q^{n-j-1}) we have k=n−j−2k=n-j-2 and ak=1a_{k}=1.

    Step 2:

    Since

    C=(q4−q3+q2)​(qn−j−qn−1)+qj+3(q−1)2,C=\frac{{\left(q^{4}-q^{3}+q^{2}\right)}{\left(q^{n-j}-q^{n}-1\right)}+q^{j+3}}{{\left(q-1\right)}^{2}},

    we have c1=0c_{1}=0. By (3.9), DD must satisfy deg⁡(D)⩽n−j−1\deg(D)\leqslant n-j-1 and

    1+q2+q3+⋯+qn−1+qn+1=D+O⁡(qj+2).1+q^{2}+q^{3}+\cdots+q^{n-1}+q^{n+1}=D+O(q^{j+2}).

    As in the previous cases, we easily find that A∗=A(m+1),B∗=B(m+1),C∗=C(m+1)A^{*}=A^{(m+1)},\ B^{*}=B^{(m+1)},\ C^{*}=C^{(m+1)}, where m+1=3​j+1m+1=3j+1 with 1⩽j⩽n−11\leqslant j\leqslant n-1.

Lemma 3.4 gives us the list of the first 3​n−23n-2 sextuplets 𝒬j\mathcal{Q}_{j} in (3.11) that are needed to write the HH-fraction of Φn\Phi_{n}. However, a simple calculation shows that the result of

𝙽𝚎𝚡𝚝𝙰𝙱𝙲⁡(A1(3​n−2),B1(3​n−2),C1(3​n−2)){\tt NextABC}\bigl(A_{1}^{(3n-2)},B_{1}^{(3n-2)},C_{1}^{(3n-2)}\bigr)

is not expressible in terms of the data that were defined Definition 3.3, and we have to define another family of data to proceed calculations.

Definition 3.5.

Let (𝒬2(m))m⩾1\bigl(\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{(m)}\bigr)_{m\geqslant 1} denote the sequence of sextuplets

𝒬2(m)=(A2(m),B2(m),C2(m),k2(m),ak2(m),D2(m))\mathcal{Q}_{2}^{(m)}=\bigl(A_{2}^{(m)},B_{2}^{(m)},C_{2}^{(m)},k_{2}^{(m)},a_{k_{2}}^{(m)},D_{2}^{(m)}\bigr)

constituted of polynomials A2(m),B2(m),C2(m),D2(m)A_{2}^{(m)},B_{2}^{(m)},C_{2}^{(m)},D_{2}^{(m)}, integers k2(m)k_{2}^{(m)} and numbers ak2(m)∈{±1}a_{k_{2}}^{(m)}\in\{\pm 1\} defined as follows:

  1. 1)

    If m=1m=1:

    A2(m)\displaystyle A_{2}^{(m)} =1+q2​[n−1]q,\displaystyle=1+q^{2}[n-1]_{q}, B2(m)\displaystyle B_{2}^{(m)} =⟨n⟩q−2​qn,\displaystyle=\langle n\rangle_{q}-2q^{n}, C2(m)\displaystyle C_{2}^{(m)} =−qn,\displaystyle=-q^{n},
    k2(m)\displaystyle k_{2}^{(m)} =0,\displaystyle=0, ak2(m)\displaystyle a_{k_{2}}^{(m)} =1,\displaystyle=1, D2(m)\displaystyle D_{2}^{(m)} =1.\displaystyle=1.
  2. 2)

    If m=4m=4:

    A2(m)\displaystyle A_{2}^{(m)} =qn−1,\displaystyle=q^{n-1}, B2(m)\displaystyle B_{2}^{(m)} =⟨n⟩q,\displaystyle=\langle n\rangle_{q}, C2(m)\displaystyle C_{2}^{(m)} =−qn+2,\displaystyle=-q^{n+2},
    k2(m)\displaystyle k_{2}^{(m)} =n−1,\displaystyle=n-1, ak2(m)\displaystyle a_{k_{2}}^{(m)} =1,\displaystyle=1, D2(m)\displaystyle D_{2}^{(m)} =⟨n⟩q+qn+1.\displaystyle=\langle n\rangle_{q}+q^{n+1}.

Lemma 3.6.

Suppose that 1⩽m⩽3​n+11\leqslant m\leqslant 3n+1. Then

𝙽𝚎𝚡𝚝𝙰𝙱𝙲⁡(A2(m),B2(m),C2(m))=(A2(m+1),B2(m+1),C2(m+1),k2(m),ak2(m),D2(m)).{\tt NextABC}\bigl(A_{2}^{(m)},B_{2}^{(m)},C_{2}^{(m)}\bigr)=\bigl(A_{2}^{(m+1)},B_{2}^{(m+1)},C_{2}^{(m+1)},k_{2}^{(m)},a_{k_{2}}^{(m)},D_{2}^{(m)}\bigr).
Proof.

As for Lemma 3.4, the proof consists in applying the algorithm NextABC for each case introduced in Definition 3.5. Calculations as exactly of the same kind, lengthy but not difficult, and we omit details here. ∎

Notice that Lemma 3.6 is not valid any more for next index m=3​n+2m=3n+2, i.e.

𝙽𝚎𝚡𝚝𝙰𝙱𝙲⁡(A2(3​n+2),B2(3​n+2),C2(3​n+2)){\tt NextABC}\bigl(A_{2}^{(3n+2)},B_{2}^{(3n+2)},C_{2}^{(3n+2)}\bigr)

will not give a sextuplet consisting of elements defined in Definition 3.5. Nevertheless, we make the following crucial observation:

A2(3​n+1)\displaystyle A_{2}^{(3n+1)} =(q2−q+1)​qn−2=A1(2),\displaystyle=(q^{2}-q+1)q^{n-2}=A_{1}^{(2)},
B2(3​n+1)\displaystyle B_{2}^{(3n+1)} =(q2−q+1)​[n]q=B1(2),\displaystyle=(q^{2}-q+1)[n]_{q}=B_{1}^{(2)},
C2(3​n+1)\displaystyle C_{2}^{(3n+1)} =−q2=C1(2),\displaystyle=-q^{2}=C_{1}^{(2)},
k2(3​n+1)\displaystyle k_{2}^{(3n+1)} =n−2=k1(2),\displaystyle=n-2=k_{1}^{(2)},
ak2(3​n+1)\displaystyle a_{k_{2}}^{(3n+1)} =1=ak1(2),\displaystyle=1=a_{k_{1}}^{(2)},
D2(3​n+1)\displaystyle D_{2}^{(3n+1)} =[n]q=D1(2),\displaystyle=[n]_{q}=D_{1}^{(2)},

and therefore

𝙽𝚎𝚡𝚝𝙰𝙱𝙲⁡(A2(3​n+1),B2(3​n+1),C2(3​n+1))=(A1(3),B1(3),C1(3),k1(2),ak1(2),D1(2)).{\tt NextABC}\bigl(A_{2}^{(3n+1)},B_{2}^{(3n+1)},C_{2}^{(3n+1)}\bigr)=\bigl(A_{1}^{(3)},B_{1}^{(3)},C_{1}^{(3)},k_{1}^{(2)},a_{k_{1}}^{(2)},D_{1}^{(2)}\bigr).

In other words we came back to the first family (𝒬1(m))\bigl(\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{(m)}\bigr) of sextuplets and this proves the periodicity of the HH-fraction expansion of Φn\Phi_{n}. Indeed, we just proved that the family (3.11) (𝒬j)j⩾0(\mathcal{Q}_{j})_{j\geqslant 0} of sextuplets associated with Φn\Phi_{n} is completely determined by the following equalities:

(3.13) first terms:𝒬j={𝒬1(j+1)if 0⩽j⩽3​n−4,𝒬2(j−3​n+4)if 3​n−3⩽j⩽6​n−4,\displaystyle\text{first terms:}\quad\mathcal{Q}_{j}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{(j+1)}&if $0\leqslant j\leqslant 3n-4$,\\ \mathcal{Q}_{2}^{(j-3n+4)}&if $3n-3\leqslant j\leqslant 6n-4,$\end{cases}
periodicity:𝒬j+6​n−4=𝒬jfor j⩾1.\displaystyle\text{periodicity:}\quad\mathcal{Q}_{j+6n-4}=\mathcal{Q}_{j}\quad\text{for }j\geqslant 1.

We summarize the results of this section in Table 3.1 below. Extracting the data sequence (kj,aj,Dj)(k_{j},a_{j},D_{j}) from that table and applying (3.10) (with p=1p=1 and p′=6​n−3p^{\prime}=6n-3) gives exactly (1.20), hence Theorem A is proved. In the table, the first line j=0j=0 corresponds to the head of the HH-fraction (first term) and the periodic part consists of the block of lines from j=1j=1 to j=6​n−4j=6n-4.

3.3. A remark on symmetries

Formula (1.20) reveals three types of symmetries inside the period of the continued fraction. Let (αi)(\alpha_{i}) and (βi)(\beta_{i}) denote the sequences of numerators and denominators of the continued fraction (1.20), respectively, i.e. write

Φn​(q)=𝒦i=0+∞⁡αiβi=α0β0+(𝒦i=16​n−4⁡αiβi+)∗.\Phi_{n}(q)=\mathop{\vphantom{\sum}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{367007}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{262148}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}}\displaylimits_{i=0}^{+\infty}\frac{\alpha_{i}}{\beta_{i}}=\frac{\alpha_{0}}{\beta_{0}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\left(\mathop{\vphantom{\sum}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{367007}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{262148}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}}\displaylimits_{i=1}^{6n-4}\frac{\alpha_{i}}{\beta_{i}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*}.
  1. 1)

    Symmetries inside the whole period (and, actually, a bit larger block):

    αi=α6​n−1−i,i=1,2,…,6n−2.\displaystyle\alpha_{i}=\alpha_{6n-1-i},\quad i=1,2,\ldots,6n-2.
    βi=β6​n−2−i,i=1,2,…,6n−3.\displaystyle\beta_{i}=\beta_{6n-2-i},\quad i=1,2,\ldots,6n-3.
  2. 2)

    Symmetries inside the first block Un​(q)U_{n}(q):

    αi=α3​n−2−i,i=1,2,…,3n−3.\displaystyle\alpha_{i}=\alpha_{3n-2-i},\quad i=1,2,\ldots,3n-3.
    β0=β3​n−3−qandβi=β3​n−3−i+χi​q,i=1,2,…,3​n−4,\displaystyle\beta_{0}=\beta_{3n-3}-q\quad\text{and}\quad\beta_{i}=\beta_{3n-3-i}+\chi_{i}q,\quad i=1,2,\ldots,3n-4,
     where ​χi={0if i≡0​(mod​ 3)1if i≡1​(mod​ 3)−1if i≡−1​(mod​ 3).\displaystyle\qquad\text{ where }\chi_{i}=\begin{cases}0&if $i\equiv 0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)$\\ 1&if $i\equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)$\\ -1&if $i\equiv-1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)$.\end{cases}

    Symmetries of type (1) and (2) imply also similar symmetries inside the block Wn​(q)W_{n}(q).

  3. 3)

    ‘Pseudo half-period’ for numerators inside the whole period:

    αi=αi+3​n+1,i=1,…,3n−3.\alpha_{i}=\alpha_{i+3n+1},\quad i=1,\ldots,3n-3.

    These identities reflect that the sequence of numerators in block Wn​(q)W_{n}(q) is essentially the same as in block Un​(q)U_{n}(q).

4. Special values and (anti-)periodicity property

As mentioned in the introduction, the statement of Theorem B for 1⩽ℓ⩽n+11\leqslant\ell\leqslant n+1 obviously follows from Theorem D and the case ℓ=0\ell=0. This section is devoted to the proof of the latter and we still assume that n⩾3n\geqslant 3.

4.1. Collecting some data

In this subsection we give the explicit values of the family of parameters (sj)(s_{j}) and (εj)(\varepsilon_{j}) introduced in (2.8) and (2.9), because they are needed to compute the Hankel determinants Δj​(Φn)\Delta_{j}(\Phi_{n}) with formula (2.10). In particular, we will emphasize on some symmetric patterns they form, because these will simplify further calculations.

First, we know from the results in Section 3.2 that the sequence (ki)(k_{i}) is (6​n−4)(6n-4)-periodic and determined by the following first values:

(4.1) {k0=0,k3​i+1=n−2−i,k3​i+2=i,k3​i+3=0,for ​i=0,…,n−2k3​n−2=n−1,k3​n−1=n,k3​n=n−1,k3​i+1=0,k3​i+2=2​n−2−i,k3​i+3=i−n,for ​i=n,…,2​n−3k6​n−5=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}k_{0}=0,&&&\\ k_{3i+1}=n-2-i,&k_{3i+2}=i,&k_{3i+3}=0,&\text{for }i=0,\ldots,n-2\\ k_{3n-2}=n-1,&k_{3n-1}=n,&k_{3n}=n-1,&\\ k_{3i+1}=0,&k_{3i+2}=2n-2-i,&k_{3i+3}=i-n,&\text{for }i=n,\ldots,2n-3\\ k_{6n-5}=0.&&&\end{array}\right.

Hence we have:

The first period of the sequence (ki)(k_{i}) admits the following symmetries:

  1. 1)

    Symmetry inside the whole period {k0,…,k6​n−3}\{k_{0},\ldots,k_{6n-3}\}:

    (4.2) ki=k6​n−2−ifor ​i=0,…,6​n−2.k_{i}=k_{6n-2-i}\quad\text{for }i=0,\ldots,6n-2.
  2. 2)

    One-to-one correspondence between subsets {k0,…,k3​n−3}\{k_{0},\ldots,k_{3n-3}\} and {k3​n+1,…,k6​n−2}\{k_{3n+1},\ldots,k_{6n-2}\} of ‘non-central’ values:

    (4.3) ki+3​n+1=kifor ​i=0,…,3​n−3.k_{i+3n+1}=k_{i}\quad\text{for }i=0,\ldots,3n-3.
  3. 3)

    Symmetries inside the subsets {k0,…,k3​n−3}\{k_{0},\ldots,k_{3n-3}\} and {k3​n+1,…,k6​n−2}\{k_{3n+1},\ldots,k_{6n-2}\}:

    (4.4) ki=k3​n−3−ifor ​i=0,…,3​n−3\displaystyle k_{i}=k_{3n-3-i}\quad\text{for }i=0,\ldots,3n-3
    k3​n+1+i=k6​n−2−ifor ​i=0,…,3​n−3.\displaystyle k_{3n+1+i}=k_{6n-2-i}\quad\text{for }i=0,\ldots,3n-3.
