Recall from (2.10) that the numbers sj∈𝒮s_{j}\in\mathcal{S} enumerate the nonzero Hankel determinants of Φn\Phi_{n}. We determine now their values:

Lemma 4.3.
  1. 1)

    The values of the parameter sjs_{j}, for 0⩽j⩽6​n−40\leqslant j\leqslant 6n-4, are given by

    s3​p\displaystyle s_{3p} ={p⁡(n+1),if 0⩽p⩽n−1,(n+1)2,if p=n,1+(p+3)​n,if n+1⩽p⩽2​n−2;\displaystyle=\begin{cases}p(n+1),&if $0\leqslant p\leqslant n-1$,\\ (n+1)^{2},&if $p=n$,\\ 1+(p+3)n,&if $n+1\leqslant p\leqslant 2n-2$;\end{cases}
    s3​p+1\displaystyle s_{3p+1} ={1+p⁡(n+1),if 0⩽p⩽n−1,n+(p+1)​(n+1),if n⩽p⩽2​n−2;\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1+p(n+1),&if $0\leqslant p\leqslant n-1$,\\ n+(p+1)(n+1),&if $n\leqslant p\leqslant 2n-2$;\end{cases}
    s3​p+2\displaystyle s_{3p+2} ={(p+1)​n,if 0⩽p⩽n−2,n⁡(n+1),if p=n−1,(p+2)​(n+1),if n⩽p⩽2​n−2.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}(p+1)n,&if $0\leqslant p\leqslant n-2$,\\ n(n+1),&if $p=n-1$,\\ (p+2)(n+1),&if $n\leqslant p\leqslant 2n-2$.\end{cases}
  2. 2)

    We have the following relations:

    (4.5) sj+3​n+1=sj+s3​n+1=sj+n+(n+1)2for ​0⩽j⩽3​n−2,\displaystyle s_{j+3n+1}=s_{j}+s_{3n+1}=s_{j}+n+(n+1)^{2}\quad\text{for }0\leqslant j\leqslant 3n-2,
    (4.6) sj+s6​n−1−j=s6​n−1=(2​n+1)​(n+1)for ​0⩽j⩽6​n−1.\displaystyle s_{j}+s_{6n-1-j}=s_{6n-1}=(2n+1)(n+1)\quad\text{for }0\leqslant j\leqslant 6n-1.
Proof.

Recall that, by definition, s0=0s_{0}=0 and sj=j+∑i=0j−1kis_{j}=j+\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}k_{i}. Thus, from the values (4.1) of the kik_{i}’s it is easy to compute first all values of sjs_{j} for 0⩽j⩽3​n+10\leqslant j\leqslant 3n+1. Then we prove (4.5) by using (4.3):

sj+3​n+1=s3​n+1+j+∑i=3​n+13​n+jki=s3​n+1+j+∑i=0j−1ki=s3​n+1+sjs_{j+3n+1}=s_{3n+1}+j+\sum_{i=3n+1}^{3n+j}k_{i}=s_{3n+1}+j+\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}k_{i}=s_{3n+1}+s_{j}

and in particular these symmetries give the remaining values of sjs_{j} for 3​n+2⩽j⩽6​n−43n+2\leqslant j\leqslant 6n-4. Similarly, the second symmetry sj+s6​n−1−j=s6​n−1s_{j}+s_{6n-1-j}=s_{6n-1} follows from (4.2) and it remains only to compute, with the help of (4.5)

s6​n−1=s3​n−2+s3​n+1=n+(n+1)2+n2=(2​n+1)​(n+1).∎s_{6n-1}=s_{3n-2}+s_{3n+1}=n+(n+1)^{2}+n^{2}=(2n+1)(n+1).\qed
Lemma 4.4.
  1. 1)

    The values of the parameter εj\varepsilon_{j}, for 0⩽j⩽6​n−40\leqslant j\leqslant 6n-4, are given by

    ε3​p\displaystyle\varepsilon_{3p} ={p​(n−p−1)​(n−1)2+p​(p−1)​(p+1)3,if 0⩽p⩽n−1,n⁡(n2+2)3,if p=n,n​(n+1)​(2​n+1)6+(p−n)​(2​n−p)​(n−2)2+(p−n)​(p−n−1)​(p−n−2)3,if n+1⩽p⩽2​n−2;\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\textstyle\frac{p(n-p-1)(n-1)}{2}+\frac{p(p-1)(p+1)}{3},&if $0\leqslant p\leqslant n-1$,\\ \textstyle\frac{n(n^{2}+2)}{3},&if $p=n$,\\ \textstyle\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}+\frac{(p-n)(2n-p)(n-2)}{2}+\frac{(p-n)(p-n-1)(p-n-2)}{3},&if $n+1\leqslant p\leqslant 2n-2$;\end{cases}
    ε3​p+1\displaystyle\varepsilon_{3p+1} ={ε3​p,if 0⩽p⩽n−1,n​(n+1)​(2​n+1)6+(p−n)​(2​n−p−1)​(n−1)2+(p−n)​(p−n−1)​(p−n+1)3,if n⩽p⩽2​n−2;\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\varepsilon_{3p},&if $0\leqslant p\leqslant n-1$,\\ \textstyle\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}+\frac{(p-n)(2n-p-1)(n-1)}{2}+\frac{(p-n)(p-n-1)(p-n+1)}{3},&if $n\leqslant p\leqslant 2n-2$;\end{cases}
    ε3​p+2\displaystyle\varepsilon_{3p+2} ={(p+1)​(n−p−1)​(n−2)2+p​(p−1)​(p+1)3,if 0⩽p⩽n−2,n​(n−1)​(2​n−1)6,if p=n−1,ε3​p+1,if n⩽p⩽2​n−2.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\textstyle\frac{(p+1)(n-p-1)(n-2)}{2}+\frac{p(p-1)(p+1)}{3},&if $0\leqslant p\leqslant n-2$,\\ \textstyle\frac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{6},&if $p=n-1$,\\ \varepsilon_{3p+1},&if $n\leqslant p\leqslant 2n-2$.\end{cases}
  2. 2)

    We have the following relations:

    (4.8) εj+ε6​n−1−j=ε6​n−1=n​(n+1)​(2​n+1)6+n​(n−1)​(n−2)3for ​0⩽j⩽6​n−1.\displaystyle\textstyle\varepsilon_{j}+\varepsilon_{6n-1-j}=\varepsilon_{6n-1}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}+\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3}\quad\text{for }0\leqslant j\leqslant 6n-1.
Proof.

Recall that εj:=∑i=0j−1ki​(ki+1)2\varepsilon_{j}:=\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\frac{k_{i}(k_{i}+1)}{2} with convention ε0:=0\varepsilon_{0}:=0. As one can guess, computations rely essentially on the values (4.1) of the kjk_{j}’s and on the classical formula

∑i=aa+b−1i⁡(i+1)=a​b​(a+b)+b​(b−1)​(b+1)3\sum_{i=a}^{a+b-1}i(i+1)=ab(a+b)+\frac{b(b-1)(b+1)}{3}

for nonnegative integers aa and bb, at least for εj\varepsilon_{j} with j⩽3​n+1j\leqslant 3n+1. The remaining cases, as in the previous lemma, will follow from the symmetry relations (4.7) and (4.8). To prove the first one, we simply use (4.3), while to prove the second one we use (4.5): we write for 1⩽j⩽6​n−11\leqslant j\leqslant 6n-1 (the remaining case j=0j=0 is trivial)

εj=∑i=0j−1ki​(ki+1)2=∑i=0j−1k6​n−2−i​(k6​n−2−i+1)2=∑i=6​n−1−j6​n−2ki​(ki+1)2\varepsilon_{j}=\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\frac{k_{i}(k_{i}+1)}{2}=\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}\frac{k_{6n-2-i}(k_{6n-2-i}+1)}{2}=\sum_{i=6n-1-j}^{6n-2}\frac{k_{i}(k_{i}+1)}{2}

ε6​n−1=ε3​n+1+ε3​n−2=n​(n+1)​(2​n+1)6+n​(n−1)​(n−2)2.∎\varepsilon_{6n-1}=\varepsilon_{3n+1}+\varepsilon_{3n-2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}+\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{2}.\qed

4.2. Proof of Theorem B in the case ℓ=0\ell=0

First we note that, when ℓ=0\ell=0, first assertion in Theorem B follows immediately from Theorem A. Indeed, we see that the sequence (vi)(v_{i}) defined in (2.7) can only have values ±1\pm 1. More precisely, using the fact that the sequence is (6​n−4)(6n-4)-periodic with offset 11, i.e. vi+6​n−4=viv_{i+6n-4}=v_{i} for all i⩾1i\geqslant 1 and by looking at the list {v0,v1,…,v6​n−4}\{v_{0},v_{1},\ldots,v_{6n-4}\} in (1.20) we get that

(4.9) vj={1if j=0, or j≡3​n−2​(mod​ 6​n−4), or j≡3​n+1​(mod​ 6​n−4),−1else.v_{j}=\begin{cases}1&if $j=0$, or $j\equiv 3n-2\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 6n-4)$, or $j\equiv 3n+1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 6n-4)$,\\ -1&else.\end{cases}

Applying formula (2.10) we deduce that Hankel determinants Δj\Delta_{j} can only take the values −1,0,1-1,0,1.

Thus, it remains to prove the second assertion in Theorem B, i.e. formula

(4.10) Δj+2​n​(n+1)=(−1)n​Δjfor all ​j⩾0.\Delta_{j+2n(n+1)}=(-1)^{n}\Delta_{j}\quad\text{for all }j\geqslant 0.

In fact, to do this, it is not even necessary to know the explicit expression of the Hankel determinants, which will be given in Section 5.

Lemma 4.5.

We have sp+6​n−4=sp+2​n​(n+1)s_{p+6n-4}=s_{p}+2n(n+1) for all p⩾0p\geqslant 0.

Proof.

By definition,

sp+6​n−4=p+6​n−4+∑i=0p−1ki=s6​n−4+p+∑i=6​n−46​n−4+pki.s_{p+6n-4}=p+6n-4+\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}k_{i}=s_{6n-4}+p+\sum_{i=6n-4}^{6n-4+p}k_{i}.

Using the (6​n−4)(6n-4)-periodicity of the sequence (ki)(k_{i}) we obtain that sp+6​n−4=s6​n−4+sps_{p+6n-4}=s_{6n-4}+s_{p}, and we read the value

(4.11) s6​n−4=2​n​(n+1)s_{6n-4}=2n(n+1)

from Lemma 4.3. ∎

From this lemma we deduce that j∈𝒮j\in\mathcal{S} if and only if j+2​n​(n+1)∈𝒮j+2n(n+1)\in\mathcal{S} and that it suffices to prove (4.10) for j∈𝒮j\in\mathcal{S} (see (2.8) for the definition of the set 𝒮\mathcal{S}). In other words, we are left to prove that

Δsp+2​n​(n+1)=(−1)n​Δspfor all ​p⩾0.\Delta_{s_{p}+2n(n+1)}=(-1)^{n}\Delta_{s_{p}}\quad\text{for all }p\geqslant 0.

This will be an immediate consequence of Lemma 4.5 and of the following result.

Proposition 4.6.

We have Δsp+6​n−4=(−1)n​Δsp\Delta_{s_{p+6n-4}}=(-1)^{n}\Delta_{s_{p}} for all p⩾0p\geqslant 0.

Proof.

First of all, note that, since parameters viv_{i} can only be ±1\pm 1 we can rewrite the expression of nonzero Hankel determinants (2.10) as follows:

(4.12) Δsp=(−1)εp(v0v1⋯vp−1)spv1s1v2s2⋯vp−1sp−1.\Delta_{s_{p}}=(-1)^{\varepsilon_{p}}(v_{0}v_{1}\cdots v_{p-1})^{s_{p}}\,v_{1}^{s_{1}}v_{2}^{s_{2}}\cdots{}v_{p-1}^{s_{p-1}}.

However, in this formula we must exclude the case p=0p=0, i.e. sp=0s_{p}=0, where Δ0=1\Delta_{0}=1 by convention, and this leads us to divide our proof into two parts.

∙\bullet Let us first suppose that p⩾1p\geqslant 1. In this case, formula (4.12) also gives

Δsp+6​n−4\displaystyle\Delta_{s_{p+6n-4}} =(−1)εp+6​n−4(v0v1⋯vp+6​n−5)sp+6​n−4v1s1v2s2⋯vp+6​n−5sp+6​n−5\displaystyle=(-1)^{\varepsilon_{p+6n-4}}\bigl(v_{0}v_{1}\cdots v_{p+6n-5})^{s_{p+6n-4}}\,v_{1}^{s_{1}}v_{2}^{s_{2}}\cdots v_{p+6n-5}^{s_{p+6n-5}}
=(−1)εp+6​n−4(v0v1⋯v6​n−4)sp+6​n−4(v6​n−3v6​n−2⋯vp+6​n−5)sp+6​n−4\displaystyle=(-1)^{\varepsilon_{p+6n-4}}\bigl(v_{0}v_{1}\cdots v_{6n-4}\bigr)^{s_{p+6n-4}}\bigl(v_{6n-3}v_{6n-2}\cdots v_{p+6n-5}\bigr)^{s_{p+6n-4}}
×(v1s1v2s2⋯v6​n−4s6​n−4)(v6​n−3s6​n−3v6​n−2s6​n−2⋯vp+6​n−5sp+6​n−5).\displaystyle\qquad\times\bigl(v_{1}^{s_{1}}v_{2}^{s_{2}}\cdots v_{6n-4}^{s_{6n-4}}\bigr)\bigl(v_{6n-3}^{s_{6n-3}}v_{6n-2}^{s_{6n-2}}\cdots v_{p+6n-5}^{s_{p+6n-5}}\bigr).

Let us simplify last expression. Firstly, because of (4.9) we have

v0v1⋯v6​n−4=(−1)6​n−3−3=1.v_{0}v_{1}\cdots v_{6n-4}=(-1)^{6n-3-3}=1.

Secondly, by using the (6​n−4)(6n-4)-periodicity of the sequence (ki)(k_{i}) we see that εp+6​n−4=ε6​n−4+εp\varepsilon_{p+6n-4}=\varepsilon_{6n-4}+\varepsilon_{p}, with

by Lemma 4.4 and we note that this is always an odd number. Thirdly, since the sequence (vi)(v_{i}) is (6​n−4)(6n-4)-periodic with values in {±1}\{\pm 1\}, since sp+6​n−4s_{p+6n-4} has same parity as sps_{p} by Lemma 4.5 and since v0=1v_{0}=1, we get

and, similarly,

v6​n−3s6​n−3v6​n−2s6​n−2⋯vp+6​n−5sp+6​n−5=v1s1v2s2⋯vp−1sp−1.v_{6n-3}^{s_{6n-3}}v_{6n-2}^{s_{6n-2}}\cdots v_{p+6n-5}^{s_{p+6n-5}}=v_{1}^{s_{1}}v_{2}^{s_{2}}\cdots v_{p-1}^{s_{p-1}}.

To sum up, so far we have proved that

=−Δsp(v1s1v2s2⋯v6​n−4s6​n−4).\displaystyle=-\Delta_{s_{p}}\bigl(v_{1}^{s_{1}}v_{2}^{s_{2}}\cdots v_{6n-4}^{s_{6n-4}}\bigr).

It remains to calculate the product in the right-hand side of this equality, which by (4.9) equals

But

with

by Lemma 4.3, and

s1+s2+⋯+s6​n−2−(s3​n−2+s3​n+1)=(3​n−2)​(2​n+1)​(n+1)s_{1}+s_{2}+\cdots+s_{6n-2}-(s_{3n-2}+s_{3n+1})=(3n-2)(2n+1)(n+1)

s1+s2+⋯+s6​n−4−s3​n−2−s3​n+1\displaystyle s_{1}+s_{2}+\cdots+s_{6n-4}-s_{3n-2}-s_{3n+1} =(3​n−2)​(2​n+1)​(n+1)−(4​n+1)​(n+1)\displaystyle=(3n-2)(2n+1)(n+1)-(4n+1)(n+1)
=(n+1)​(6​n2−5​n−3).\displaystyle=(n+1)(6n^{2}-5n-3).

by (4.12). But the integer ε6​n−4\varepsilon_{6n-4} is odd by (4.13) and the integer s6​n−4s_{6n-4} is even by (4.11). Together with the result of (4.16) this yields

5. The Hankel determinants Δj​(Φn)\Delta_{j}(\Phi_{n})

Recall from (2.10) that the nonzero Hankel determinants Δj\Delta_{j} are exactly the ones for which j∈𝒮j\in\mathcal{S}, i.e. j=sqj=s_{q} for some integer q⩾0q\geqslant 0. We give now their explicit values, taking into account that it suffices to restrict ourselves to a finite subsequence of length 2​n​(n+1)2n(n+1) which is the period when nn is even (resp. the anti-period when nn is odd), by the results proved in the previous section.

Theorem 5.1.

    (5.3) Δs3​p+2\displaystyle\Delta_{s_{3p+2}} ={(−1)(p+1)​n⁡(n−1)2,if 0⩽p⩽n−2,(−1)n​(n−1)22,if p=n−1,(−1)p​n⁡(n−1)2​(−1)(p+1)​(p+2)2,if n⩽p⩽2​n−3.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}(-1)^{(p+1)\frac{n(n-1)}{2}},&if $0\leqslant p\leqslant n-2$,\\ (-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)^{2}}{2}},&if $p=n-1$,\\ (-1)^{p\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}(-1)^{\frac{(p+1)(p+2)}{2}},&if $n\leqslant p\leqslant 2n-3$.\end{cases}

It is important to note that, since (2​n+1)​(n+1)(2n+1)(n+1) is strictly greater than the length of the (anti-)period 2​n​(n+1)2n(n+1), symmetry (5.4) holds inside the whole first (anti-)period.

Remark 5.3.

Figure 5.1 helps us to visualize the repartition of zero Hankel determinants, in particular we can observe the existence of subsets formed with kk consecutive zeros for k=1,2,3,4,5k=1,2,3,4,5. Using the results of Lemma 4.3, it is not difficult to see that this is a general phenomenon: for any k∈{1,…,n}k\in\{1,\ldots,n\} there exists a set of kk successive zero Hankel determinants, and the case k=nk=n occurs exactly once, between the nonzero determinants Δs3​n−1\Delta_{s_{3n-1}} and Δs3​n\Delta_{s_{3n}}. Actually this maximal set of nn successive zero determinants is also the only one which is invariant under the symmetry (5.4) (see fig. 5.1 for case n=5n=5; the 55 consecutive zero determinants are Δ31\Delta_{31}, Δ32\Delta_{32}, Δ33\Delta_{33}, Δ34\Delta_{34} and Δ35\Delta_{35}).

6. The Gale-Robinson relations

Assume as usual that n⩾3n\geqslant 3. For any integer j⩾0j\geqslant 0 and any ℓ∈{0,1,…,n+1}\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,n+1\}, set

Γj(ℓ):=Δj(ℓ)​Δj+2​n+2(ℓ)−Δj+1(ℓ)​Δj+2​n+1(ℓ)+(Δj+n+1(ℓ))2.\Gamma_{j}^{(\ell)}:=\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)}\,\Delta_{j+2n+2}^{(\ell)}-\Delta_{j+1}^{(\ell)}\,\Delta_{j+2n+1}^{(\ell)}+\bigl(\Delta_{j+n+1}^{(\ell)}\bigr)^{2}.

We want to prove the Gale-Robinson recurrence stated in Theorem C, which reads

(6.1) Γj(ℓ)=0for all j⩾0 and all ℓ∈{0,1,…,n+1}.\Gamma_{j}^{(\ell)}=0\qquad\text{for all $j\geqslant 0$ and all $\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,n+1\}$}.

Assuming the validity of Theorem D (to be proved in Section 7) it is easily checked that

Γj(ℓ+1)=Γj(ℓ),\Gamma_{j}^{(\ell+1)}=\Gamma_{j}^{(\ell)},

so that it suffices to prove (6.1) in the case ℓ=0\ell=0, and this will be our purpose in this section.

For simplicity we put Γj:=Γj(0)\Gamma_{j}:=\Gamma_{j}^{(0)}. Because of the (anti-)periodicity property shown in Theorem B, it remains to show that

(6.2) Γj=0for ​0⩽j⩽2​n​(n+1)−1,\Gamma_{j}=0\quad\text{for }0\leqslant j\leqslant 2n(n+1)-1,

where

Γj:=Δj​Δj+2​n+2−Δj+1​Δj+2​n+1+(Δj+n+1)2.\Gamma_{j}:=\Delta_{j}\,\Delta_{j+2n+2}-\Delta_{j+1}\,\Delta_{j+2n+1}+\bigl(\Delta_{j+n+1}\bigr)^{2}.

By Lemma 4.3 we know which Hankel determinants are nonzero and, by the previous theorem, we know the explicit values of these nonzero determinants, so we just have to check that Γj\Gamma_{j} vanishes in any case. Adding and multiplying five Hankel determinants Δi\Delta_{i} which can be either −1-1, 00 or 11 is certainly a triviality but the difficulty comes from the fact that we have to handle them simultaneously, and there is no clue of how their values are connected in general. In fact, we will distinguish four cases, looking at pairs of successive determinants (Δj,Δj+1)(\Delta_{j},\Delta_{j+1}) and discussing on the nullity of one of them, in order to simplify the expression of Γj\Gamma_{j} when possible. And, because (6.2) must be checked for j⩽2​n​(n+1)−1j\leqslant 2n(n+1)-1 we will have to discuss on Hankel determinants Δi\Delta_{i} with index

i=j+2​n+2⩽2​n​(n+1)−1+2​n+2=2​n​(n+2)+1,i=j+2n+2\leqslant 2n(n+1)-1+2n+2=2n(n+2)+1,

i.e. we need the description of the intersection 𝒮∩{0,1,…,2​n​(n+2)+1}\mathcal{S}\cap\{0,1,\ldots,2n(n+2)+1\}. One the one hand, Lemma 4.3 implies the characterization:

(6.3) j∈𝒮​ and ​0⩽j⩽2​n​(n+1)⇔j​ satisfies one of the conditions (i)-(v)j\in\mathcal{S}\text{ and }0\leqslant j\leqslant 2n(n+1)\iff j\text{ satisfies one of the conditions (i)-(v)}

where

  1. (i)

    s3​n+1=n+(n+1)2,s3​n+2=(n+2)​(n+1),s3​n+3=1+(n+4)​n.s_{3n+1}=n+(n+1)^{2},\quad s_{3n+2}=(n+2)(n+1),\quad s_{3n+3}=1+(n+4)n.

    In the first case, we have j+1=(n+1)2∈𝒮j+1=(n+1)^{2}\in\mathcal{S} by (6.3), hence Δj+1≠0\Delta_{j+1}\neq 0, contradiction. In the second case, we have j=(n+1)2∈𝒮j=(n+1)^{2}\in\mathcal{S} and Δj≠0\Delta_{j}\neq 0, also a contradiction. In the third case we have j+1=n+(n+1)2∈𝒮j+1=n+(n+1)^{2}\in\mathcal{S} and Δj+1≠0\Delta_{j+1}\neq 0, still a contradiction.

  3. (c)

    Suppose now that n+(n+1)​(n+2)=s3​n+4⩽j+n+1⩽s6​n−4=2​n​(n+1)n+(n+1)(n+2)=s_{3n+4}\leqslant j+n+1\leqslant s_{6n-4}=2n(n+1). Then j+n+1j+n+1 satisfies conditions (i) or (iii) or (v) of (6.3), which implies that either jj satisfies (i) or j+1j+1 satisfies (i) or j+1j+1 satisfies (v). This leads in all cases to Δj=0\Delta_{j}=0 or Δj+1=0\Delta_{j+1}=0, a contradiction.

  4. (d)

    To finish the proof, suppose that j+n+1⩾s6​n−3=2​n2+2​n+1j+n+1\geqslant s_{6n-3}=2n^{2}+2n+1 (see (4.14)). Since j⩽2​n​(n+1)−1j\leqslant 2n(n+1)-1 one also has j+n+1⩽(2​n+1)​(n+1)−1=2​n2+3​n=s6​n−2j+n+1\leqslant(2n+1)(n+1)-1=2n^{2}+3n=s_{6n-2} by (4.15). In other words, j+n+1∈{s6​n−2,s6​n−3}={2​n2+2​n+1,2​n2+3​n}j+n+1\in\{s_{6n-2},s_{6n-3}\}=\{2n^{2}+2n+1,2n^{2}+3n\}. Therefore, either j=2​n2+n+1=s6​n−6j=2n^{2}+n+1=s_{6n-6} or j=2​n2+2​n−1=s6​n−5j=2n^{2}+2n-1=s_{6n-5}. In both cases Δj≠0\Delta_{j}\neq 0, contradiction.

We thus have completely established Theorem C in case ℓ=0\ell=0.

7. The shifted case

In this section we give a proof of Theorems D and F. Let us recall that the contiguity relations (1.22) contained in Theorem D allow us to reduce the proofs of Theorems B and C to the case ℓ=0\ell=0 that has been treated in the previous sections.

7.1. The HH-fraction expansion for Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)} when ℓ∈{0,1,…,n+1}\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,n+1\}

The contiguity relations (1.22) stress the links which exist between Hankel determinants

Δj(ℓ−1)=Δj(ℓ−1)(Φn)=Δj(Φn(ℓ−1))andΔj(ℓ)=Δj(ℓ)(Φn)=Δj(Φn(ℓ))\Delta_{j}^{(\ell-1)}=\Delta_{j}^{(\ell-1)}(\Phi_{n})=\Delta_{j}\bigl(\Phi_{n}^{(\ell-1)}\bigl)\quad\text{and}\quad\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)}=\Delta_{j}^{(\ell)}(\Phi_{n})=\Delta_{j}\bigl(\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}\bigl)

of two consecutive shifts Φn(ℓ−1)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell-1)} and Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)} of Φn\Phi_{n}. To establish these relations we will first state the analogue of Theorem A for the shifted function Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}.

Lemma 7.1.

Suppose that

F⁡(q)=f0+f1​q+f2​q2+⋯F(q)=f_{0}+f_{1}q+f_{2}q^{2}+\cdots

is a quadratic power series satisfying the equation

where A,B,CA,B,C are polynomials (with C≠0C\neq 0). Then the shifted series

F(1)​(q)=f1+f2​q+⋯=F⁡(q)−f0qF^{(1)}(q)=f_{1}+f_{2}q+\cdots=\frac{F(q)-f_{0}}{q}

is also quadratic, satisfying the equation

A′+B′​F(1)+C′​(F(1))2=0A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}F^{(1)}+C^{\prime}\bigl(F^{(1)}\bigr)^{2}=0

with A′,B′,C′A^{\prime},B^{\prime},C^{\prime} polynomials given by

A′\displaystyle A^{\prime} =1q​(A+f0​B+f02​C),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{q}(A+f_{0}B+f_{0}^{2}C),
B′\displaystyle B^{\prime} =B+2​f0​C,\displaystyle=B+2f_{0}C,
C′\displaystyle C^{\prime} =q​C.\displaystyle=qC.
Proof.

Inserting F=q​F(1)+f0F=qF^{(1)}+f_{0} in equation (7.1) gives immediately

(7.2) A+f0​B+f02​C+q⁡(B+2​f0​C)​F(1)+q2​C​(F(1))2=0.A+f_{0}B+f_{0}^{2}C+q(B+2f_{0}C)F^{(1)}+q^{2}C\bigl(F^{(1)}\bigr)^{2}=0.

Now, the constant term in the left-hand side of (7.1) is A⁡(0)+B⁡(0)​F​(0)+C⁡(0)​F​(0)2A(0)+B(0)F(0)+C(0)F(0)^{2}, and this is actually also the constant term of the polynomial A+f0​B+f02​CA+f_{0}B+f_{0}^{2}C. Thus it equals zero, and the whole left-hand side of (7.2) can be divided by qq. ∎

We use this lemma to derive the following generalization of (2.5) which gives the quadratic equations satisfied by the shifts of Φn\Phi_{n}.

Proposition 7.2.

Let ℓ∈{0,1,…,n+1}\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,n+1\}. The ℓ\ell-shift Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)} of the qq-metallic number Φn\Phi_{n} is also a quadratic power series with integer coefficients, satisfying the equation

(7.3) A(ℓ)+B(ℓ)​Φn(ℓ)+C(ℓ)​(Φn(ℓ))2=0,A^{(\ell)}+B^{(\ell)}\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}+C^{(\ell)}\bigl(\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}\bigr)^{2}=0,

where A(ℓ),B(ℓ),C(ℓ)A^{(\ell)},B^{(\ell)},C^{(\ell)} are polynomials with integer coefficients given as follows: for 0≤ℓ≤n0\leq\ell\leq n,

A(ℓ)\displaystyle A^{(\ell)} =qℓ+1−(q2−q+1)​(qn−qn−ℓ+1)(q−1)2,\displaystyle=\frac{q^{\ell+1}-(q^{2}-q+1)(q^{n}-q^{n-\ell}+1)}{(q-1)^{2}},
B(ℓ)\displaystyle B^{(\ell)} =2​qℓ+1−(q2−q+1)​(qn+1)q−1,\displaystyle=\frac{2q^{\ell+1}-(q^{2}-q+1)(q^{n}+1)}{q-1},
C(ℓ)\displaystyle C^{(\ell)} =qℓ+1,\displaystyle=q^{\ell+1},

and for ℓ=n+1\ell=n+1,

A(n+1)\displaystyle A^{(n+1)} =−qn−1,\displaystyle=-q^{n-1},
B(n+1)\displaystyle B^{(n+1)} =−(q2−q+1)+(q2−3​q+1)​qnq−1,\displaystyle=-\frac{(q^{2}-q+1)+(q^{2}-3q+1)q^{n}}{q-1},
C(n+1)\displaystyle C^{(n+1)} =qn+2.\displaystyle=q^{n+2}.
Proof.

We proceed by induction on ℓ∈{0,…,n+1}\ell\in\{0,\ldots,n+1\}.

∙\bullet We already know that (7.3) is true for ℓ=0\ell=0, by (2.5).

∙\bullet Assume that (7.3) is valid for some ℓ∈{0,…,n−1}\ell\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}. By (2.6), the constant term of Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)} equals 11. According to Lemma 7.1 we have

A(ℓ+1)+B(ℓ+1)​Φn(ℓ)+C(ℓ+1)​(Φn(ℓ))2=0A^{(\ell+1)}+B^{(\ell+1)}\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}+C^{(\ell+1)}\bigl(\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}\bigr)^{2}=0

with

C(ℓ+1)=1q​(A(ℓ)+B(ℓ)+C(ℓ)),B(ℓ+1)=B(ℓ)+2​C(ℓ),C(ℓ+1)=q​C(ℓ).C^{(\ell+1)}=\frac{1}{q}\bigl(A^{(\ell)}+B^{(\ell)}+C^{(\ell)}\bigr),\quad B^{(\ell+1)}=B^{(\ell)}+2C^{(\ell)},\quad C^{(\ell+1)}=qC^{(\ell)}.

A simple calculation ensures that these formulas for A(ℓ+1),B(ℓ+1),C(ℓ+1)A^{(\ell+1)},B^{(\ell+1)},C^{(\ell+1)} coincide actually with the expressions given in the statement, at rank ℓ+1\ell+1.

∙\bullet Finally, when ℓ=n\ell=n we have

A(n)=−qn,B(n)=−(q2−q+1)+(q2−3​q+1)​qnq−1,C(n)=qn+1.A^{(n)}=-q^{n},\quad B^{(n)}=-\frac{(q^{2}-q+1)+(q^{2}-3q+1)q^{n}}{q-1},\quad C^{(n)}=q^{n+1}.

We apply again Lemma 7.1, but this time with f0=0f_{0}=0 since the constant term of Φn(n)\Phi_{n}^{(n)} equals 00. We easily see that A(n+1),B(n+1),C(n+1)A^{(n+1)},B^{(n+1)},C^{(n+1)} admit the required expressions. ∎

The key point is that we have already encountered the family of polynomials A(ℓ),B(ℓ),C(ℓ)A^{(\ell)},B^{(\ell)},C^{(\ell)}. Indeed, with notations of Definitions 3.3 and 3.5 and (3.13):

A(0)\displaystyle A^{(0)} =A1(1)=A0,\displaystyle=A_{1}^{(1)}=A_{0}, B(0)\displaystyle B^{(0)} =B1(1)=B0,\displaystyle=B_{1}^{(1)}=B_{0}, C(0)\displaystyle C^{(0)} =C1(1)=C0,\displaystyle=C_{1}^{(1)}=C_{0},
A(ℓ)\displaystyle A^{(\ell)} =−A1(3​ℓ+1)=−A3​ℓ,\displaystyle=-A_{1}^{(3\ell+1)}=-A_{3\ell}, B(ℓ)\displaystyle B^{(\ell)} =B1(3​ℓ+1)=B3​ℓ,\displaystyle=B_{1}^{(3\ell+1)}=B_{3\ell}, C(ℓ)\displaystyle C^{(\ell)} =−C1(3​ℓ+1)=−C3​ℓ,\displaystyle=-C_{1}^{(3\ell+1)}=-C_{3\ell},
for ​ℓ=1,2,…,n−2,\displaystyle\qquad\text{for }\ell=1,2,\ldots,n-2,
A(n−1)\displaystyle A^{(n-1)} =−A2(1)=−A3​n−3,\displaystyle=-A_{2}^{(1)}=-A_{3n-3}, B(n−1)\displaystyle B^{(n-1)} =B2(1)=B3​n−3,\displaystyle=B_{2}^{(1)}=B_{3n-3}, C(n−1)\displaystyle C^{(n-1)} =−C2(1)=−C3​n−3,\displaystyle=-C_{2}^{(1)}=-C_{3n-3},
A(n)\displaystyle A^{(n)} =−A2(3)=−A3​n−1,\displaystyle=-A_{2}^{(3)}=-A_{3n-1}, B(n)\displaystyle B^{(n)} =B2(3)=B3​n−1,\displaystyle=B_{2}^{(3)}=B_{3n-1}, C(n)\displaystyle C^{(n)} =−C2(3)=−C3​n−1,\displaystyle=-C_{2}^{(3)}=-C_{3n-1},
A(n+1)\displaystyle A^{(n+1)} =−A2(4)=−A3​n,\displaystyle=-A_{2}^{(4)}=-A_{3n}, B(n+1)\displaystyle B^{(n+1)} =B2(4)=B3​n,\displaystyle=B_{2}^{(4)}=B_{3n}, C(n+1)\displaystyle C^{(n+1)} =−C2(4)=−C3​n.\displaystyle=-C_{2}^{(4)}=-C_{3n}.

(Notice that the minus signs appearing here are due to the minus sign in the first numerator of a HH-fraction constructed with the algorithm NextABC, see (3.10).) From these identities we deduce that the HH-fraction expansions of the shifts Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}, 1⩽ℓ⩽n+11\leqslant\ell\leqslant n+1, can be borrowed from Lemmas 3.4 and 3.6 as for the case ℓ=0\ell=0. The difference lies in the initialization of algorithm NextABC. Namely, denoting by

mℓ:={3​ℓif 0⩽ℓ⩽n−1,3​n−1if ℓ=n,3​nif ℓ=n+1,m_{\ell}:=\begin{cases}3\ell&if $0\leqslant\ell\leqslant n-1$,\\ 3n-1&if $\ell=n$,\\ 3n&if $\ell=n+1$,\end{cases}

one must initialize NextABC with the triple (Aml,Bml,Cml)(A_{m_{l}},B_{m_{l}},C_{m_{l}}) to get the HH-fraction of Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}. In other words, the HH-fraction of Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)} when 1⩽ℓ⩽n+11\leqslant\ell\leqslant n+1 is obtained from the one of Φn(0)=Φn\Phi_{n}^{(0)}=\Phi_{n} by truncating the first mℓm_{\ell} terms, and by adjusting the power of the monomial in the first numerator: because of (3.10), it must be set to kmℓk_{m_{\ell}} instead of kmℓ−1+kmℓ+2k_{m_{\ell-1}}+k_{m_{\ell}}+2.

To sum up the discussion, we have proved the following analogue of Theorem A.

7.2. The contiguity relations

Let us proceed with a reformulation of Theorem 7.3. Recall that the HH-fraction components Un,Vn,WnU_{n},V_{n},W_{n} of Φn\Phi_{n} were defined in Theorem A and set

Un(ℓ)​(q)={11−q+𝒦i=ℓn−3⁡(qn−i[n−i]q+qn[i+2]q−q+qi+21−q)+q2[2]q+qn[n]q−q+qn1,if 0⩽ℓ⩽n−3;11−q+q2[2]q+qn[n]q−q+qn1,if ℓ=n−2;1q,if ℓ=n−1;0,if ℓ=n or ℓ=n+1,U_{n}^{(\ell)}(q)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{1-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\mathop{\vphantom{\sum}\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{524296}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{367007}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}{\vbox{\hbox{\resizebox{}{262148}{$\mathcal{K}$}}}}}\displaylimits_{i=\ell}^{n-3}\left(\frac{q^{n-i}}{[n-i]_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{n}}{[i+2]_{q}-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{i+2}}{1-q}\right)\\[-4.0pt] \qquad\qquad\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{2}}{[2]_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{n}}{[n]_{q}-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{n}}{1},&if $0\leqslant\ell\leqslant n-3$;\\ \frac{1}{1-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{2}}{[2]_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{n}}{[n]_{q}-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{n}}{1},&if $\ell=n-2$;\\ \frac{1}{q},&if $\ell=n-1$;\\ 0,&if $\ell=n$ or $\ell=n+1$,\end{cases}

and

Vn(ℓ)​(q)={Vn​(q),if 0⩽ℓ⩽n−1;qn⟨n⟩q+q2​n+1⟨n⟩q+qn+1+−qn+11,if ℓ=n;qn−1⟨n⟩q+qn+1+−qn+11,if ℓ=n+1.V_{n}^{(\ell)}(q)=\begin{cases}V_{n}(q),&if $0\leqslant\ell\leqslant n-1$;\\ \frac{q^{n}}{\langle n\rangle_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{2n+1}}{\langle n\rangle_{q}+q^{n+1}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-q^{n+1}}{1},&if $\ell=n$;\\ \frac{q^{n-1}}{\langle n\rangle_{q}+q^{n+1}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-q^{n+1}}{1},&if $\ell=n+1$.\end{cases}

Then Theorem 7.3 says exactly that, for any ℓ∈{0,1,…,n+1}\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,n+1\}, we have:

Φn(ℓ)​(q)=Un(ℓ)​(q)+Vn(ℓ)​(q)+(Wn​(q)+Un​(q)+Wn​(q)+)∗.\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}(q)=U_{n}^{(\ell)}(q)\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,V_{n}^{(\ell)}(q)\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\left(W_{n}(q)\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,U_{n}(q)\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,W_{n}(q)\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\right)^{*}.

From this expression we derive immediately the following consequence.

Corollary 7.5.

Contiguity relations for Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}.
If ℓ∈{0,1,…,n−2}\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-2\} then

Φn(ℓ)​(q)=11−q+qn−ℓ[n−ℓ]q+qn[ℓ+2]q−q+qℓ+2​Φn(ℓ+1)​(q).\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}(q)=\frac{1}{1-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{n-\ell}}{[n-\ell]_{q}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{q^{n}}{[\ell+2]_{q}-q}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,q^{\ell+2}\,\Phi_{n}^{(\ell+1)}(q).

For the two remaining cases we have

Φn(n−1)​(q)=11+−qn+1⟨n⟩q+qn+1+qn+1​Φn(n)​(q).\Phi_{n}^{(n-1)}(q)=\frac{1}{1}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,\frac{-q^{n+1}}{\langle n\rangle_{q}+q^{n+1}}\,\mathrel{\raisebox{0.83333pt}{$+$}}\,q^{n+1}\,\Phi_{n}^{(n)}(q).

and

Φn(n)​(q)=qn⟨n⟩q+qn+2​Φn(n+1)​(q).\Phi_{n}^{(n)}(q)=\frac{q^{n}}{\langle n\rangle_{q}+q^{n+2}\,\Phi_{n}^{(n+1)}(q)}.

We now read the effect of these relations on Hankel determinants.

Proof of Theorem D.

We treat separately three cases.

  • ∙\bullet

    Assume first that ℓ∈{0,1,…,n−2}\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-2\}, so that we have, by the previous corollary:

    (7.4) Φn(ℓ)​(q)=11−q−q2​G1​(q)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}(q)=\frac{1}{1-q-q^{2}\,G_{1}(q)}

    where

    (7.5) G1​(q)=−qn−ℓ−21+q+⋯+qn−ℓ−1−qn−ℓ​G2​(q)G_{1}(q)=\frac{-q^{n-\ell-2}}{1+q+\cdots+q^{n-\ell-1}-q^{n-\ell}\,G_{2}(q)}

    and

    (7.6) G2​(q)=−qℓ1+q2+q3+⋯+qℓ+1−qℓ+2​(−Φn(ℓ+1)​(q)).G_{2}(q)=\frac{-q^{\ell}}{1+q^{2}+q^{3}+\cdots+q^{\ell+1}-q^{\ell+2}\,\bigl(-\Phi_{n}^{(\ell+1)}(q)\bigr)}.

    Now we point out the following result.

    Lemma 7.6 (Lemma 2.2 of [Han16]).

    Let kk be a nonnegative integer and let F⁡(q),G⁡(q)F(q),G(q) be two power series such that

    F⁡(q)=qk1+q​u​(q)−qk+2​G​(q)F(q)=\frac{q^{k}}{1+q\,u(q)-q^{k+2}\,G(q)}

    where u⁡(q)u(q) is a polynomial such that deg⁡(u)⩽k\deg(u)\leqslant k. Then, Δj​(G)=(−1)k⁡(k+1)2​Δj+k+1​(F).\Delta_{j}(G)=(-1)^{\frac{k(k+1)}{2}}\,\Delta_{j+k+1}(F).

    Applying this lemma successively to (7.6), (7.5) and (7.4) we get

    Δj​(Φn(ℓ+1))\displaystyle\Delta_{j}(\Phi_{n}^{(\ell+1)}) =(−1)j​Δj​(−Φn(ℓ+1))\displaystyle=(-1)^{j}\Delta_{j}(-\Phi_{n}^{(\ell+1)})
    =(−1)j​(−1)ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)2​Δj+ℓ+1​(−G2)\displaystyle=(-1)^{j}(-1)^{\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{2}}\Delta_{j+\ell+1}(-G_{2})
    =(−1)j​(−1)ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)2​(−1)j+ℓ+1​Δj+ℓ+1​(G2),\displaystyle=(-1)^{j}(-1)^{\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{2}}(-1)^{j+\ell+1}\Delta_{j+\ell+1}(G_{2}),

    as well as

    Δj+ℓ+1​(G2)\displaystyle\Delta_{j+\ell+1}(G_{2}) =(−1)(n−ℓ−2)​(n−ℓ−1)2​Δj+n​(−G1)\displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{(n-\ell-2)(n-\ell-1)}{2}}\Delta_{j+n}(-G_{1})
    =(−1)(n−ℓ−2)​(n−ℓ−1)2​(−1)j+n​Δj+n​(G1)\displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{(n-\ell-2)(n-\ell-1)}{2}}(-1)^{j+n}\Delta_{j+n}(G_{1})

    and

    Δj+n​(G1)=Δj+n+1​(Φn(ℓ)).\Delta_{j+n}(G_{1})=\Delta_{j+n+1}(\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}).

    Gathering these formulas we obtain

    Δj​(Φn(ℓ+1))=(−1)f⁡(n,ℓ,j)​Δj+n+1​(Φn(ℓ))\Delta_{j}(\Phi_{n}^{(\ell+1)})=(-1)^{f(n,\ell,j)}\Delta_{j+n+1}(\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)})

    where

    f⁡(n,ℓ,j)\displaystyle f(n,\ell,j) =j+ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)2+j+ℓ+1+(n−ℓ−2)​(n−ℓ−1)2+j+n\displaystyle=j+\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{2}+j+\ell+1+\frac{(n-\ell-2)(n-\ell-1)}{2}+j+n
    =ℓ⁡(ℓ+3)2+1+(n−ℓ−2)​(n−ℓ−1)2+3​j+n.\displaystyle=\frac{\ell(\ell+3)}{2}+1+\frac{(n-\ell-2)(n-\ell-1)}{2}+3j+n.

    But

    (n−ℓ−2)​(n−ℓ−1)\displaystyle(n-\ell-2)(n-\ell-1) =n⁡(n−ℓ−2)−ℓ⁡(n−ℓ−2)−(n−ℓ−2)\displaystyle=n(n-\ell-2)-\ell(n-\ell-2)-(n-\ell-2)
    =n⁡(n−2​ℓ−3)+ℓ⁡(ℓ+3)+2,\displaystyle=n(n-2\ell-3)+\ell(\ell+3)+2,

    hence

    f⁡(n,ℓ,j)\displaystyle f(n,\ell,j) =ℓ⁡(ℓ+3)2+1+n⁡(n−2​ℓ−3)2+ℓ⁡(ℓ+3)2+1+3​j+n\displaystyle=\frac{\ell(\ell+3)}{2}+1+\frac{n(n-2\ell-3)}{2}+\frac{\ell(\ell+3)}{2}+1+3j+n
    ≡n⁡(n−2​ℓ−3)2+j+n⁡(mod​ 2)\displaystyle\equiv\frac{n(n-2\ell-3)}{2}+j+n\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2)
    ≡n⁡(n+2​ℓ−1)2+j⁡(mod​ 2),\displaystyle\equiv\frac{n(n+2\ell-1)}{2}+j\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2),

    and this last formula implies the contiguity relation (1.22) when ℓ=0,1,…,n−2\ell=0,1,\ldots,n-2.

  • ∙\bullet

    Assume now that ℓ=n−1\ell=n-1. By Corollary 7.5 and (1.19) we have

    Φn(n−1)​(q)=11−q2​G3​(q)\Phi_{n}^{(n-1)}(q)=\frac{1}{1-q^{2}G_{3}(q)}

    with

    G3​(q)=qn−11+q2+q3+⋯+qn−1+2​qn−qn+1​Φn(n)​(q).G_{3}(q)=\frac{q^{n-1}}{1+q^{2}+q^{3}+\cdots+q^{n-1}+2q^{n}-q^{n+1}\,\Phi_{n}^{(n)}(q)}.

    Applying Lemma 7.6 we get

    Δj​(Φn(ℓ))\displaystyle\Delta_{j}(\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}) =(−1)j​Δj​(−Φn(ℓ))\displaystyle=(-1)^{j}\Delta_{j}(-\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)})
    =(−1)j​(−1)n⁡(n−1)2​Δj+n​(G1)\displaystyle=(-1)^{j}(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\Delta_{j+n}(G_{1})
    =(−1)j​(−1)n⁡(n−1)2​Δj+n+1​(Φn(n−1)).\displaystyle=(-1)^{j}(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\Delta_{j+n+1}(\Phi_{n}^{(n-1)}).

    It is easily seen that this is exactly (1.22) for ℓ=n−1\ell=n-1.

  • ∙\bullet

    Lastly, assume that ℓ=n\ell=n. By Corollary 7.5 and (1.19) we have

    Φn(n)​(q)=qn1+q2+q3+⋯+qn−1+2​qn−qn+1−qn+2​(−Φn(n+1)​(q)).\Phi_{n}^{(n)}(q)=\frac{q^{n}}{1+q^{2}+q^{3}+\cdots+q^{n-1}+2q^{n}-q^{n+1}-q^{n+2}\,\bigl(-\Phi_{n}^{(n+1)}(q)\bigr)}.

    Again, applying Lemma 7.6 yields

    Δj​(Φn(n+1))=(−1)j​Δj​(−Φn(n+1))=(−1)j​(−1)n⁡(n+1)2​Δj+n+1​(Φn(n))\Delta_{j}(\Phi_{n}^{(n+1)})=(-1)^{j}\Delta_{j}(-\Phi_{n}^{(n+1)})\\ =(-1)^{j}(-1)^{\frac{n(n+1)}{2}}\Delta_{j+n+1}(\Phi_{n}^{(n)})

    which is the same as (1.22) when ℓ=n\ell=n.

This finishes our proof of Theorem D in all cases. ∎

Example 7.7.

To illustrate the result of Theorem D, let us consider as usual the case n=5n=5. We have, for all j⩾0j\geqslant 0:

Δj(1)\displaystyle\Delta_{j}^{(1)} =(−1)j​Δj+6,\displaystyle=(-1)^{j}\Delta_{j+6}, Δj(2)\displaystyle\Delta_{j}^{(2)} =(−1)j+1​Δj+6(1)=−Δj+12,\displaystyle=(-1)^{j+1}\Delta_{j+6}^{(1)}=-\Delta_{j+12},
Δj(3)\displaystyle\Delta_{j}^{(3)} =(−1)j​Δj+6(2)=(−1)j+1​Δj+18,\displaystyle=(-1)^{j}\Delta_{j+6}^{(2)}=(-1)^{j+1}\Delta_{j+18}, Δj(4)\displaystyle\Delta_{j}^{(4)} =(−1)j+1​Δj+6(3)=Δj+24,\displaystyle=(-1)^{j+1}\Delta_{j+6}^{(3)}=\Delta_{j+24},
Δj(5)\displaystyle\Delta_{j}^{(5)} =(−1)j​Δj+6(4)=(−1)j​Δj+30,\displaystyle=(-1)^{j}\Delta_{j+6}^{(4)}=(-1)^{j}\Delta_{j+30}, Δj(6)\displaystyle\Delta_{j}^{(6)} =(−1)j+1​Δj+6(5)=−Δj+36.\displaystyle=(-1)^{j+1}\Delta_{j+6}^{(5)}=-\Delta_{j+36}.

We see that all sequences Δ(ℓ)\Delta^{(\ell)} are expressed in terms of the first (non shifted) one Δ=Δ(0)\Delta=\Delta^{(0)} (remind fig. 5.1), using a translation of n+1=6n+1=6 units and a function which changes possibly the signs. Figures 7.1, 7.2 and 7.3 highlight in particular the translation of the center of the symmetry (the blank circle) when ℓ=1,2,3\ell=1,2,3.

7.3. The shifted case, modulo pp

We end our article by proving Theorem F. Fix a prime number pp and let ℓ⩾0\ell\geqslant 0. Since Φn(ℓ)​(q)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}(q) is a power series with integer coefficients, according to Theorem 1.1 of [Han16], the statement of Theorem F reduces to prove that Φn(ℓ)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)} satisfies a quadratic functional equation

A(ℓ)+B(ℓ)​Φn(ℓ)+C(ℓ)​(Φn(ℓ))2=0A^{(\ell)}+B^{(\ell)}\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}+C^{(\ell)}\bigl(\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}\bigr)^{2}=0

with three polynomials A(ℓ),B(ℓ),C(ℓ)∈ℤ⁡[X]A^{(\ell)},B^{(\ell)},C^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{Z}[X] such that

B(ℓ)​(0)=1,C(ℓ)≠0,C(ℓ)​(0)=0.B^{(\ell)}(0)=1,\quad C^{(\ell)}\neq 0,\quad C^{(\ell)}(0)=0.

Let us actually prove that such an equation holds with

(7.7) B(ℓ)​(0)=1,C(ℓ)=qℓ+1.B^{(\ell)}(0)=1,\quad C^{(\ell)}=q^{\ell+1}.

We proceed by induction on ℓ⩾0\ell\geqslant 0. By (2.5), it is clear that conditions (7.7) are fulfilled for ℓ=0\ell=0. Now, assume that they are true for some ℓ⩾0\ell\geqslant 0. By Lemma 7.1 we know that Φn(ℓ+1)\Phi_{n}^{(\ell+1)} satisfies the quadratic equation

A(ℓ+1)+B(ℓ+1)​Φn(ℓ+1)+C(ℓ+1)​(Φn(ℓ+1))2=0A^{(\ell+1)}+B^{(\ell+1)}\Phi_{n}^{(\ell+1)}+C^{(\ell+1)}\bigl(\Phi_{n}^{(\ell+1)}\bigr)^{2}=0

with A(ℓ+1),B(ℓ+1),C(ℓ+1)∈ℤ⁡[X]A^{(\ell+1)},B^{(\ell+1)},C^{(\ell+1)}\in\mathbb{Z}[X] satisfying

B(ℓ+1)=B(ℓ)+2​Φn(ℓ)​(0)​C(ℓ),C(ℓ+1)=q​C(ℓ).B^{(\ell+1)}=B^{(\ell)}+2\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}(0)C^{(\ell)},\quad C^{(\ell+1)}=qC^{(\ell)}.

By induction hypothesis, this gives

C(ℓ+1)=qℓ+2,B(ℓ+1)​(0)=B(ℓ)​(0)+2​Φn(ℓ)​(0)​C(ℓ)​(0)=1,C^{(\ell+1)}=q^{\ell+2},\quad B^{(\ell+1)}(0)=B^{(\ell)}(0)+2\Phi_{n}^{(\ell)}(0)C^{(\ell)}(0)=1,

as required.
